variables.why: Changing a single bond to a double bond rearranges bonds between the same carbons. No carbon is added or removed.

why.correct: Phospholipids are amphipathic. Water molecules attract the charged, polar heads and hydrogen-bond strongly with each other, so they push the nonpolar tails together, away from water. Two layers, tails facing inward, keep every head in water and every tail out of it.
options: The tails of neighboring phospholipids are not covalently bonded. They cluster because water squeezes them together.
The heads are charged and polar, which is why they face the water. It is the tails that are nonpolar.
The tails are fatty acid chains of carbon and hydrogen, which carry no charges.
Correct. The arrangement comes from water holding on to itself and to the heads, not from the tails attracting each other strongly.

why.correct: Structure builds level by level. The sequence (primary) comes first; local helices and sheets (secondary) form from backbone hydrogen bonds; side chains then fold the whole chain (tertiary); and finally separate folded chains assemble (quaternary).

Heat shakes molecules hard enough to break hydrogen bonds and other weak attractions that hold a protein's secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure. The protein unfolds (denatures) and loses its function. The covalent peptide bonds survive, so the amino acid sequence stays the same.
options: Correct. Denaturation changes shape, not sequence, and shape is what lets a protein work.
Peptide bonds are strong covalent bonds. Breaking them takes hydrolysis, as in digestion, not a few degrees of extra heat.
Heat does not rebuild amino acids into sugars. The proteins are still present, just unfolded.
Heat does not change the chemical makeup of side chains. It breaks the weak attractions between them.

why.correct: Denaturation breaks the weak bonds that hold a protein's shape, not the peptide bonds of its backbone. The unfolded chains stay whole and tangle with each other, which is why cooked egg white is solid.
options: This step is right. Heat is molecular motion, and faster motion strains the weak bonds in the protein.
This step is right. Hydrogen bonds are weak enough for heat to break, which unfolds the protein.
This is the error. The chains remain whole; if they fell apart into free amino acids, they could not tangle into a solid.
This step is right. Unfolded chains expose parts that stick to other chains, forming a solid mesh.

why.correct: Water hydrogen-bonds with itself and with polar and charged side chains, which face outward. Nonpolar side chains are hydrophobic, so the fold tucks them together in the middle, away from water.
options: A nonpolar surface would be pushed into clusters by water, the way oil is. Polar and charged side chains face the water instead.
Correct. Hydrophobic side chains cluster in the center, like oil droplets forming in water.
Side chains are covalently part of each amino acid, and amino acids are held in the chain by peptide bonds. Folding does not release them.
Nonpolar side chains attract water only weakly. It is polar and charged side chains that interact with water.

why.correct: Every nucleotide has a phosphate group, a five-carbon sugar (ribose or deoxyribose) and a nitrogen-containing base.
options: Those are the parts of an amino acid, the monomer of proteins.
Glycerol plus fatty acids builds a lipid. A phospholipid adds a phosphate head, but it has no base.
Four fused carbon rings define a steroid, such as cholesterol.
Correct. Phosphate, sugar and base together make one nucleotide.

why.correct: Ribose and uracil both mark ribonucleic acid. Deoxyribonucleic acid uses deoxyribose and thymine in their place.
options: Correct. Ribose sugar and the base uracil are found in ribonucleic acid.
Deoxyribonucleic acid has deoxyribose, one oxygen short of ribose, and uses thymine instead of uracil.
Ribose is a sugar, but a polysaccharide is a chain of sugars alone. A strand with bases is built of nucleotides.
A polypeptide is a chain of amino acids. It has no sugar or nitrogenous bases in its backbone.

why.correct: Hydrolysis adds water across the bond to the outermost phosphate. That leaves ADP (adenosine diphosphate) plus a free phosphate and releases energy the cell uses for work. The cell later rebuilds ATP from ADP and phosphate.
options: The adenine and ribose stay in place. Only the outermost phosphate is removed.
Adding a phosphate would take energy in rather than release it. Cells release energy by removing one.
Correct. ATP plus water gives ADP, phosphate and usable energy.
ATP works as a single nucleotide. Its energy comes from losing a phosphate, not from joining a chain.

why.correct: Triglycerides are packed with carbon–hydrogen bonds, so they hold about 9 kcal per gram against about 4 for carbohydrate. Being hydrophobic, they are stored with almost no water, while glycogen holds a lot of water with it. Both facts pack more energy into each gram of stored tissue.
options: Triglycerides are hydrophobic and do not dissolve in blood. Their value is compact storage, not ready solubility.
Triglycerides are glycerol plus fatty acids. Branched glucose polymers describe glycogen.
Triglycerides contain only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. Their energy comes from their many carbon–hydrogen bonds.
Correct. High energy per gram plus very little stored water make fat the compact long-term store.

why.correct: Building a polymer from monomers is dehydration synthesis. Each new bond between glucose units releases one water molecule, and thousands of links make a branched glycogen molecule.
options: Hydrolysis splits molecules apart. Building glycogen joins glucose units, the opposite reaction.
Correct. Joining monomers releases water, and repeated joining builds glycogen.
Denaturation describes proteins losing their shape. Glucose is joined into glycogen by new covalent bonds.
Peptide bonds join amino acids in proteins. Glucose units in glycogen are joined by a different covalent bond.

why.correct: Proteins are built from 20 kinds of amino acid. Amino groups supply nitrogen, and the side chains of a few amino acids, such as cysteine, contain sulfur.
options: Correct. Twenty kinds of unit plus nitrogen and sulfur point to a chain of amino acids.
Carbohydrates contain only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, and their units are sugars.
A triglyceride is glycerol plus three fatty acids, and it has no nitrogen or sulfur. It is not built from 20 kinds of unit.
Nucleic acids contain phosphorus rather than sulfur, and each is built from four kinds of nucleotide, not 20 kinds of unit.

why.correct: Extra hydrogen ions attach to charged side chains and change their charges. Ionic bonds between oppositely charged side chains then fail, the protein's fold loosens and it denatures. The covalent backbone is untouched.
options: Peptide bonds are covalent and are not broken by a change in hydrogen ion concentration. The sequence stays the same.
The covalent bonds inside side chains stay intact. What changes is whether a side chain carries a charge.
Correct. Changing side-chain charges breaks the ionic bonds that help hold the fold.
Carbon–hydrogen bonds are strong, nonpolar covalent bonds. Hydrogen ions do not break them.

why.correct: An acid is a hydrogen ion donor: it releases H+ when it dissolves, raising the fluid's H+ concentration and lowering its pH.
options: Taking up hydrogen ions is what a base does. It lowers the H+ concentration.
Correct. Releasing H+ is the defining property of an acid.
That describes a salt, such as sodium chloride, which releases neither H+ nor OH−.
Resisting a change in pH is what a buffer does, using a weak acid and a weak base together.

why.correct: The pH values differ by 2 units, and each unit is a factor of ten: 10 × 10 = 100. The lower pH is the more acidic fluid, so the urine at pH 5 holds 100 times more hydrogen ions.
options: Two errors: the scale is not linear, and a higher pH means fewer hydrogen ions, not more.
The direction is right, but the pH scale counts in powers of ten. Two units is 100-fold, not 2-fold.
The size is right, but the direction is reversed. Lower pH means more hydrogen ions.
Correct. Two units of pH is a hundredfold difference, and the lower pH has more H+.

why.correct: pH is the negative log of [H+]. The log of 10⁻⁵ is −5, and the minus sign makes it 5. A pH below 7 is acidic.
options: A pH of 9 would mean [H+] = 10⁻⁹ mol/L, far fewer hydrogen ions than this solution has. This subtracts 5 from 14, which is not the formula.
The number is right, but a pH below 7 means more H+ than OH−, which is acidic.
Correct. −log(10⁻⁵) = 5, and 5 is below neutral 7.
The minus sign in pH = −log[H+] flips the negative power into a positive number, so pH is 5, not −5.

why.correct: pH fell by 0.30 units. Because log 2 is about 0.3, a fall of 0.3 doubles [H+]: from about 40 nmol/L at pH 7.40 to about 80 nmol/L at 7.10.
options: Correct. A 0.3 fall in pH is a doubling of hydrogen ions, from about 40 to about 80 nmol/L.
About 4% is the change in the pH number itself (0.3 out of 7.4). The pH scale is logarithmic, so the hydrogen ion change is far larger.
Halving would go with a rise in pH of 0.3. His pH fell, so hydrogen ions went up.
A 30-fold change reads the 0.30 as if each tenth were tenfold. Only a whole unit is tenfold; 0.3 units is twofold.

why.correct: Normal arterial blood pH is 7.35 to 7.45, slightly basic. That is a hydrogen ion concentration of only about 35 to 45 nmol/L.
options: 6.80 to 7.00 is far below normal. Blood that acidic is at the edge of what people survive.
7.00 is neutral, as in pure water. Blood is kept slightly basic.
Correct. Blood pH sits in the narrow band from 7.35 to 7.45.
7.80 to 8.00 is far above normal, at or beyond the edge of what people survive.

why.correct: Acidemia is blood pH below 7.35. At 7.29 her blood holds more hydrogen ions than normal. The process causing it is an acidosis.
options: Alkalemia is blood pH above 7.45. Hers is below the normal range.
Normal is 7.35 to 7.45. A value of 7.29 is below that band.
Neutral is pH 7.00. Her blood is still slightly basic in chemical terms, but it is too acidic for blood.
Correct. Below 7.35 is acidemia.

why.correct: Stomach fluid is rich in hydrogen ions. Losing it repeatedly removes acid from the body, so hydrogen ions in the blood fall and pH rises toward alkalemia. Tingling and cramps are typical of alkalemia, which makes nerves and muscles fire too easily.
options: Correct. Losing acid raises blood pH, an alkalosis, and his symptoms fit alkalemia.
Losing an acid takes hydrogen ions away, which raises pH. It does not lower it.
The hydrogen ions in stomach fluid are secreted there from the body's own fluids. Losing them changes what is left in the blood.
More hydroxide would take up hydrogen ions and raise pH, not lower it. His problem is a loss of acid.

why.correct: Many amino acid side chains gain or lose a hydrogen ion as [H+] changes, which changes their charge. That disturbs the ionic bonds holding each protein's fold. Shape sets function, and proteins do almost every job in a cell, so many functions change together.
options: Peptide bonds are covalent and are not broken by these pH changes. The weak bonds that hold the fold are what change.
Lipids are nonpolar and are not dissolved by hydrogen ions. The effect runs through protein shape.
Correct. Changed charges disturb protein folding, and changed shape means changed function.
Water is the solvent of blood at any pH. The pH effect acts on protein shape, not on water.

why.correct: In plain water, every added hydrogen ion stays free, so pH falls steeply. In the buffered beaker, bicarbonate takes up the hydrogen ions and becomes carbonic acid, so bicarbonate falls and carbonic acid rises.

variables.name: Free hydrogen ions in the unbuffered water
variables.why: Nothing in plain water takes up the added H+, so every hydrogen ion the strong acid releases stays free.

variables.name: Bicarbonate in the buffered beaker
variables.why: Bicarbonate takes up the added hydrogen ions, and each one it takes up turns one bicarbonate into carbonic acid.

variables.name: Carbonic acid in the buffered beaker
variables.why: Each bicarbonate that takes up a hydrogen ion becomes a carbonic acid molecule, so carbonic acid rises.

variables.name: pH of the unbuffered water
variables.why: Added H+ stays free, so [H+] rises steeply and the pH plunges, in this case by several whole units.

why.correct: The H+ from the acid and the OH− from the base join into water. The leftover Na+ and Cl− are a salt, sodium chloride. This is neutralization.
options: Correct. Acid plus base gives a salt plus water.
No electrons are transferred to make neutral hydrogen gas or sodium metal. The ions simply pair up differently.
No carbon is present in either reactant, so no carbonic acid can form.
A buffer needs a weak acid and its weak base. HCl and NaOH are strong, and they cancel each other out.

why.correct: The weak base bicarbonate takes up added H+ first, forming the weak acid carbonic acid, which keeps free H+ low. Carbonic acid then splits into carbon dioxide and water, and exhaling the carbon dioxide removes the acid from the body.
Bicarbonate is the weak base of the pair: it takes up hydrogen ions, which is how it forms carbonic acid. Releasing more hydrogen ions would push pH further down, the opposite of buffering.
options: This step is right. A strong acid releases nearly all of its hydrogen ions.
This is the error. Bicarbonate takes up hydrogen ions; carbonic acid is the partner that releases them when a base is added.
This step is right. Carbonic acid is weak, so it keeps most of the hydrogen ions it received.
This step is right. Because most of the added H+ is held, the pH falls only slightly.

why.correct: Hydrogen chloride is a strong acid: nearly every unit releases its H+, so [H+] is close to 0.01 mol/L and pH is about 2. Carbonic acid is weak and releases only a small share, so its [H+] is much lower and its pH higher.
options: pH depends on the free hydrogen ions, not on how much acid was added. Strong and weak acids release very different shares.
Holding on to hydrogen ions leaves fewer free, which means a higher pH, not a lower one.
Correct. More free H+ means a lower pH, and the strong acid frees nearly all of its hydrogen ions.
The number of atoms in a molecule does not set pH. What matters is how many hydrogen ions are released into the water.

why.correct: A buffer holds acid rather than removing it, and every hydrogen ion bicarbonate takes up converts one bicarbonate into carbonic acid. While bicarbonate is plentiful, pH barely moves. Once the store runs low, new acid has little to take it up, so pH falls sharply.
options: A buffer does not create acid. His falling bicarbonate shows it was taking up hydrogen ions, as a buffer should.
Correct. Buffers have a limited capacity, set by how much weak base is left.
Bicarbonate is a weak base and stays one at any level. It becomes carbonic acid, a weak acid, only by taking up H+.
The pH scale is logarithmic at every value. The sudden drop comes from losing buffer, not from a change in the scale.

why.correct: When a base removes hydrogen ions, the weak acid of the buffer pair releases more. Carbonic acid gives up H+, which replaces what was lost, and becomes bicarbonate. Free H+ falls only a little, so pH rises only a little.
options: Bicarbonate is the weak base of the pair; releasing more base would push pH higher. The weak acid does the work here.
Breathing out carbon dioxide removes carbonic acid, which would raise pH further, not blunt the rise.
Sodium chloride and similar salts neither take up nor release H+. The buffer pair here is carbonic acid and bicarbonate.
Correct. The weak acid gives back hydrogen ions, which is the other half of how a buffer works.

why.correct: Bicarbonate takes up H+ directly to become carbonic acid. Sodium hydroxide releases OH−, and OH− joins H+ to form water. Sodium chloride is a salt and hydrogen chloride is an acid.
options: A base. Bicarbonate takes up a hydrogen ion and becomes carbonic acid.
Not a base. Sodium chloride is a salt: it separates into Na+ and Cl−, neither of which takes up or releases H+.
A base. It separates into Na+ and OH−, and each OH− takes up a hydrogen ion.
Not a base. Hydrogen chloride releases H+ in water, which makes it a strong acid.
A base. Hydroxide joins a hydrogen ion to form water.

why.correct: In pure water, 0.001 mol of freed H+ in a liter gives [H+] = 10⁻³ mol/L, pH 3. In blood, bicarbonate takes up nearly all of it and breathing removes the carbon dioxide formed, so the pH falls by only a few hundredths.
options: Blood is buffered. Bicarbonate takes up most of the added H+, so blood does not approach pH 3.
Correct. Unbuffered water swings by four whole pH units; buffered blood barely moves.
The acid already in blood is mostly held as weak carbonic acid alongside plenty of bicarbonate. That pair is what resists the change.
In pure water, 1 mL of strong acid raises [H+] ten-thousandfold, from 10⁻⁷ to 10⁻³ mol/L.

why.correct: A higher pH means fewer hydrogen ions. At 7.4, blood holds about 40 nmol/L of H+, against 100 nmol/L in pure water, so blood is slightly basic.
options: The scale runs backward: a higher pH means fewer hydrogen ions, not more.
Equal hydrogen ions would mean equal pH. Blood's pH is 0.4 units higher.
The pH difference, 0.4, is not a count of hydrogen ions. And because blood's pH is higher, it has fewer, not more.
Correct. pH 7.4 is on the basic side of neutral, about 40 nmol/L of H+ against 100 in pure water.

why.correct: A pH of 7.52 is above 7.45: alkalemia. Alkalemia makes nerves and muscles fire too easily, producing tingling around the mouth and in the fingers, cramps and spasms.
options: Correct. Overexcitable nerves and muscles are the signature of alkalemia.
Drowsiness and coma come from acidemia, which depresses the nervous system. Her pH is high.
Weaker heart contractions go with acidemia. Her pH is on the alkaline side.
The normal range ends at 7.45. A value of 7.52 is above it.

why.correct: An enzyme lowers the activation energy, the energy hill between reactants and products. It leaves the starting and ending energies, and so everything that depends on them, unchanged.
options: Correct. The active site holds substrates in a strained, well-aligned position, which lowers the energy needed to reach the transition state.
The energy released depends only on how much energy the reactants and products hold. The enzyme changes neither, so the energy released is the same with or without it.
An enzyme speeds the forward and reverse reactions by the same factor. Equilibrium is reached sooner, but at the same balance point.

Whether a reaction is exergonic or endergonic is set by the energy of its reactants and products. An enzyme cannot make an endergonic reaction release energy; that reaction still needs energy, usually from ATP.

why.correct: Fomepizole occupies the active site of alcohol dehydrogenase, so methanol cannot bind. The first step of the pathway is blocked, so little formaldehyde and formic acid form, and the unchanged methanol is removed slowly from the body.
options: Fomepizole slows an enzyme; it does not speed anything. The harmful products come from the enzyme's own action, so blocking the enzyme is what protects him.
Correct. Blocking the active site stops the first oxidation, so the acid that would lower his pH and damage his vision is not made.

Fomepizole acts on the enzyme, not on acid already in the blood. Acid that has formed has to be handled by the blood's buffers and other treatment. This is why it is given early, before acid builds up.
An inhibitor does not move a reaction's equilibrium. It lowers how fast the enzyme converts substrate, in both directions.

why.correct: A competitive inhibitor and the substrate compete for the same active site. When substrate greatly outnumbers the inhibitor, substrate wins most encounters, so more active sites are doing the reaction and the rate rises.
options: That describes a noncompetitive or permanent inhibitor. A competitive inhibitor binds the active site and comes off again; it does not change the enzyme's shape.
The substrate is what the active site is built to bind, so more substrate means more reactions, not fewer. Crowding does not block the site.
Correct. The inhibitor's effect depends on how often it, rather than the substrate, occupies the active site. Flooding the site with substrate outcompetes it.
The rate was low because the inhibitor occupied many active sites and substrate was scarce, not because every active site was busy with substrate. There was room to speed up.

why.correct: The reactants start at the same energy and the products end at the same energy in both panels. So the energy released is identical. Only the hill between them changes.
options: This is what differs: the hill is much lower with the enzyme. That lower activation energy is the whole effect of the enzyme.
A lower hill lets far more molecules react each second, so the rate is much higher with the enzyme.
Correct. The enzyme does not change the starting or ending energy, so the energy released per reaction is the same.
A faster reaction reaches equilibrium sooner. The balance point is the same, but the time to reach it is shorter with the enzyme.

why.correct: Most human enzymes work best near 37 °C. Sustained heat well above that denatures them, so activity falls sharply, but the chemistry of the reaction itself, including the energy it releases, is unchanged.

variables.name: Enzyme molecules with a working active site
variables.why: Heat far above 37 °C breaks the hydrogen bonds that hold the enzyme's folded shape. The protein unfolds (denatures), and its active site loses the shape the substrate fits.

variables.name: Rate of the catalyzed reaction
variables.why: With fewer working active sites, fewer substrate molecules are converted each second. The speed-up from faster molecular motion is far outweighed by the loss of working enzyme.

variables.name: Energy released per reaction (products compared with reactants)
variables.why: The energy released is set by the energy held in the reactants and products. Neither the enzyme nor its shape changes that; they change only how fast the reaction runs.

why.correct: With substrate scarce, more substrate raises the rate. Warming toward the enzyme's optimum speeds collisions without denaturing it. More enzyme means more active sites. An inhibitor and a pH far from the optimum both slow the enzyme.
options: Raises the rate. With little substrate, many active sites sit empty, so more substrate fills them.
Raises the rate. Warming from 30 °C to 37 °C makes molecules move faster and collide more often, and it stays at the temperature where a human enzyme keeps its shape.
Lowers the rate. A competitive inhibitor occupies active sites that the substrate would otherwise use.
Raises the rate. More enzyme molecules mean more active sites working at once.
Lowers the rate. Extra H+ changes the charges on amino acids in and around the active site, so the substrate binds and reacts less well.

why.correct: Binding comes first, and binding triggers the small shape change called induced fit. The closed active site lowers the activation energy, so the reaction occurs. The products fit poorly and leave, and because the enzyme is not used up, it is free to bind another substrate.
Catabolism releases energy, and part of it is captured by rebuilding ATP from ADP and phosphate. That ATP is then hydrolyzed to power anabolic reactions such as protein building.
options: Correct. Rebuilding ATP is how energy released by catabolism is captured and carried to the reactions that need it.
Splitting ATP is the next step in the chain, not the missing one. ATP has to be made before it can be split.
Building glycogen is itself an anabolic, energy-requiring reaction. It uses energy rather than capturing it for protein building.
Enzymes lower activation energy; they do not add energy. They come out of each reaction unchanged.

why.correct: Methanol loses electrons (with the hydrogen atoms) as it becomes formaldehyde, so it is oxidized, not reduced. NAD+ is the molecule that gains them and is reduced.
options: This step is right. The substrate binds the active site first.
This step is right. Dehydrogenases remove hydrogen atoms, and their electrons go with them.
This is the error. Losing electrons is oxidation, so methanol is oxidized to formaldehyde.
This step is right. NAD+ is the electron carrier; gaining two electrons and one H+ makes it NADH, so NAD+ is reduced.
This step is right. Enzymes are not used up, so the enzyme can bind another methanol molecule.

why.correct: Joining small molecules into a large one is anabolism. Building a larger, more ordered molecule takes energy in, so the reaction is endergonic; your cells pay for it with ATP.
options: Catabolism breaks molecules down. Linking glucose into glycogen builds a larger molecule, and it takes energy rather than releasing it.
Building glycogen is anabolic, but it takes in energy, so it is endergonic, not exergonic.
The reaction does take energy in, but it builds a larger molecule, so it is anabolic, not catabolic.
Correct. It builds a larger molecule (anabolic) and needs an energy input (endergonic).

why.correct: At equilibrium, both reactions keep running, but at the same rate, so the amounts of reactants and products stop changing.
options: Molecules keep reacting in both directions. Nothing changes overall only because each forward reaction is matched by a reverse one.
The amounts stay constant, but they are rarely equal. Many reactions settle with far more product than reactant, or the reverse.
Correct. Equal rates in both directions is what equilibrium means.
An enzyme speeds both directions by the same factor, so the balance point, and the amount of product, stays the same.

why.correct: Removing a product of a reversible reaction makes the reaction run toward it. Here carbon dioxide is removed, so the whole chain shifts left and H+ is used up.

variables.name: Carbon dioxide in the blood
variables.why: Faster, deeper breathing carries carbon dioxide out of the blood and out of the body faster than cells add it.

variables.name: Carbonic acid in the blood
variables.why: Removing carbon dioxide pulls the reversible reaction to the left: carbonic acid breaks down into carbon dioxide and water to replace what was lost.

variables.name: H+ concentration in the blood
variables.why: As carbonic acid is used up, H+ combines with bicarbonate to re-form it, so free H+ falls.

variables.name: Blood pH
variables.why: pH rises as H+ concentration falls.

why.correct: Once every active site is busy almost all the time, the enzyme is working at its maximum rate. More substrate has nowhere to bind. Only more enzyme would raise the rate.
options: Correct. With every active site busy, the enzyme cannot convert substrate any faster.
Substrate binds the active site; it does not unfold the enzyme. Denaturation comes from heat, extreme pH and similar changes.
Whether a reaction releases or needs energy depends on its reactants and products, not on how much substrate is present.
Nothing in the question suggests the substrate is an acid. The rate levels off even when pH is held constant, because the active sites are full.

why.correct: NAD+ is the coenzyme that accepts electrons when many molecules are oxidized. Without enough niacin, cells make too little NAD+, so every enzyme that depends on it as an electron carrier slows.
options: Phosphorylation of glucose uses ATP and a magnesium cofactor, not NAD+.
Hydrogen bonds form between parts of the protein chain itself. They do not need a vitamin-derived coenzyme.
Correct. These oxidations need NAD+ to accept the electrons, so they slow when NAD+ is scarce.
ATP hydrolysis is done by ATPases and uses water, not NAD+.

why.correct: A cofactor is any non-protein helper an enzyme needs. A coenzyme is the organic (carbon-based) kind. A metal ion such as Mg2+ is a cofactor, but it is not organic, so it is not a coenzyme.
options: NAD+ is an organic molecule made from niacin, so it is a coenzyme (and therefore also a cofactor).
FAD is an organic molecule made from riboflavin, so it is a coenzyme.
The substrate is the molecule the enzyme acts on, not a helper that lets the enzyme work.
Correct. A metal ion is an inorganic cofactor, so it is not a coenzyme.

why.correct: The energy released is the difference between the reactants (ATP and water) and the products (ADP and phosphate surrounded by water). The products are more stable, so they hold less energy, and the difference is released.
options: Breaking a bond always takes energy. The release comes from the new, more stable arrangement of the products, not from the bond breaking.
Correct. ATP's crowded negative phosphates make it a high-energy molecule; the products are more stable and lower in energy.
An ATPase is an enzyme. It lowers the activation energy for the reaction but adds no energy of its own.
ATP hydrolysis releases heat to its surroundings rather than taking it up.

why.correct: Each enzyme works best at its own optimum pH. Moving far from it changes the charges on amino acids in the active site and can change the enzyme's shape, so activity drops.
options: Correct. Far fewer H+ at pH 7.4 changes the charges the active site relies on, so this enzyme works poorly.
Blood's pH suits enzymes whose optimum is near neutral. This enzyme's optimum is near 2, so pH 7.4 is far from its best.
pH changes the charges on the enzyme's own amino acids, especially in the active site, so the enzyme is affected directly.
Enzymes are not used up at any pH. A pH change slows an enzyme by changing its charges and shape.

why.correct: Enzymes are catalysts: they are not used up, they speed both directions equally, and their activity depends on the shape of the active site. They add no energy and do not move equilibrium.
options: True. A catalyst leaves a reaction unchanged, so one enzyme molecule can act again and again.
True. Lowering the activation energy lowers the hill in both directions.
False. An endergonic reaction still needs energy, usually from ATP. The enzyme only lowers the activation energy.
False. Because both directions speed up equally, the balance point stays the same; it is only reached sooner.
True. The substrate must fit the active site, which depends on how the protein is folded.

why.correct: A phosphate group leaves ATP and joins glucose in the same reaction. Parts of two molecules trade places, which is an exchange reaction. It is also a phosphorylation of glucose.
options: No free phosphate is released; the phosphate goes straight onto glucose. That is why this is not simple ATP hydrolysis.
The product is glucose phosphate, a single glucose carrying a phosphate, not a chain of glucose.
No electrons move between the molecules here; a phosphate group does. ATP is not an electron carrier.
Correct. A group trades places between two molecules, which is the definition of an exchange reaction.

why.correct: NADH loses electrons, so it is oxidized (back to NAD+). Molecule X gains them, so it is reduced. Oxidation and reduction happen together in every redox reaction.
options: This reverses the two. The molecule that gives up electrons is oxidized; the one that receives them is reduced.
One molecule's loss is the other's gain, so one is oxidized and the other is reduced.
Correct. Oxidation is loss of electrons (NADH) and reduction is gain (molecule X).
A transfer of electrons is a redox reaction. Both molecules change: NADH becomes NAD+, and molecule X gains energy along with the electrons.

why.correct: Bulk flow is driven by a pressure gradient: the fluid moves from the higher-pressure end toward the lower-pressure end.
options: A concentration gradient moves individual dissolved particles, not the whole fluid. Blood moves as a whole because of a pressure difference.
Correct. A pressure difference between two points pushes the whole fluid from higher to lower pressure.
A high pressure with no difference produces no flow, as in a closed hose. What matters is how much higher the pressure is at one end than at the other.
Viscosity is part of resistance. It opposes flow rather than driving it.

why.correct: First find the pressure gradient: ΔP = 100 − 20 = 80 mm Hg. Then F = ΔP / R = 80 ÷ 4 = 20 mL/min.
options: This divides the starting pressure alone by the resistance (100 ÷ 4). Flow depends on the pressure difference, 80 mm Hg, not the starting pressure.
This multiplies the pressure gradient by the resistance (80 × 4). Resistance holds flow back, so you divide by it.
Correct. ΔP = 80 mm Hg, and 80 ÷ 4 = 20 mL/min.
This adds the two pressures (100 + 20 = 120) and divides by 4. The gradient is the difference between the pressures, not their sum.

why.correct: Resistance depends on 1 ÷ radius to the fourth power. Halving the radius makes the radius to the fourth power (½)⁴ = 1/16 as large, so resistance becomes 16 times larger. With ΔP unchanged, F = ΔP / R becomes 1/16 of the original.
options: This treats flow as simply proportional to radius. Resistance depends on the fourth power of the radius, so the effect is far larger.
This squares the radius (½ × ½). Resistance depends on the radius multiplied by itself four times, not twice.
Flow depends on both the pressure gradient and resistance. Narrowing the tube raises resistance, so flow falls even though the pressures are unchanged.
Correct. Half the radius gives 16 times the resistance, so one-sixteenth of the flow.

why.correct: Doubling the radius makes the radius to the fourth power 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16 times larger, so resistance falls to 1/16. With the same ΔP, flow becomes 16 times larger.
options: Flow does not scale directly with radius. Radius acts through its fourth power.
Correct. Resistance falls to one-sixteenth, so flow rises 16-fold.
Four times would come from squaring the radius. The rule uses the fourth power.
This is the effect of halving the radius. A wider vessel has less resistance, so flow goes up, not down.

why.correct: Flow depends on the pressure difference. Tube A has ΔP = 150 − 140 = 10 mm Hg; tube B has ΔP = 40 − 10 = 30 mm Hg. With the same resistance, tube B carries three times the flow.
options: High pressures with a small difference drive little flow. Tube A's gradient is only 10 mm Hg.
Identical tubes have the same resistance, but their pressure gradients differ (10 versus 30 mm Hg), so their flows differ.
Correct. 30 mm Hg ÷ 10 mm Hg = 3, and with equal resistance, flow is proportional to ΔP.
Fluid flows whenever one end is at a higher pressure than the other. The outlet does not need to be at 0.

why.correct: Hydrostatic pressure rises with the height of the fluid column: about 0.74 mm Hg per centimeter. Going from 50 to 100 cm adds roughly 37 mm Hg at the catheter. The pressure in the vein is unchanged, so ΔP grows and so does flow.
options: Correct. A taller column means more hydrostatic pressure at the catheter, so a larger ΔP drives more flow.
Viscosity depends on the fluid itself and its temperature, not on the bag's height.
The catheter radius is fixed by the device. Raising the bag changes pressure, not resistance.
Lifting the bag is over in a moment, but the faster flow lasts as long as the bag stays high. What persists is the extra hydrostatic pressure from the taller column.

why.correct: Flow depends on the radius to the fourth power. Doubling the radius cuts resistance to 1/16, so flow rises about 16-fold. Doubling the pressure or halving the length each only doubles flow, and a quarter less viscosity raises flow by about one-third.
options: Flow is proportional to ΔP, so doubling the pressure doubles flow: a real gain, but far smaller than the radius change.
Resistance is proportional to length, so half the length halves resistance and doubles flow.
Correct. Twice the radius gives one-sixteenth the resistance and about 16 times the flow.
Resistance is proportional to viscosity. Cutting viscosity to three-quarters raises flow by a factor of 4/3, about 33%.

why.correct: Narrowing a tube raises its resistance steeply. With the pressure gradient fixed, flow falls.

variables.name: Resistance of the tube
variables.why: A smaller radius means more friction between the fluid and the wall for the fluid passing through, and resistance depends on 1 ÷ radius to the fourth power.

variables.name: Pressure gradient between inlet and outlet
variables.why: The inlet and outlet pressures are held constant, so their difference does not change.

variables.name: Flow through the tube
variables.why: F = ΔP / R. The same ΔP divided by a larger R gives less flow.

why.correct: Resistance is set by the tube and the fluid: length, viscosity and radius. Pressures change the gradient, not the resistance.
options: Increases resistance. Resistance is proportional to length.
Does not change resistance. It raises the pressure gradient, which increases flow through the same resistance.
Increases resistance. Resistance is proportional to viscosity.
Increases resistance, steeply, because resistance depends on 1 ÷ radius to the fourth power.
Does not change resistance. A lower outlet pressure widens the pressure gradient and increases flow.

why.correct: The muscle narrows the radius. Because resistance depends on 1 ÷ radius to the fourth power, a small narrowing raises resistance a lot. With ΔP fixed, F = ΔP / R falls.
Rearranging F = ΔP / R gives R = ΔP ÷ F. With ΔP = 80 mm Hg and F = 20 mL/min, R = 80 ÷ 20 = 4.
options: This divides flow by the pressure gradient, which inverts the relationship. It gives 0.25, not 4.
This uses the inlet pressure instead of the pressure difference. Resistance is calculated from ΔP.
Correct. ΔP ÷ F = 80 ÷ 20 = 4 mm Hg for each mL/min.
Multiplying gives 1,600. Resistance is the pressure gradient divided by the flow.

why.correct: Resistance depends on 1 ÷ radius to the fourth power. If the radius to the fourth power is 1/16 as large, resistance is 16 times larger (32, not 4), and flow becomes 80 ÷ 32 = 2.5 mL/min.
options: This step is right: 80 ÷ 2 = 40 mL/min.
This step is right. It sets up a fair comparison by changing one thing only.
This step is right: ½ × ½ × ½ × ½ = 1/16.
This is the error. A radius term 1/16 as large makes resistance 16 times larger, not twice as large.
This step is right. The flow equation still applies; only R has changed.

why.correct: Body pressures are given relative to atmospheric pressure. The first number is the peak pressure during a heartbeat, 120 mm Hg above the pressure of the air around you.
options: Correct. The reading is relative to atmospheric pressure, and the higher number is the peak during each beat.
Atmospheric pressure alone is about 760 mm Hg at sea level. Readings leave it out and give only the pressure above it.
The unit is millimeters of mercury, not blood. Mercury is about 13.6 times denser than water, so a column of blood at the same pressure would be far taller.
Arterial blood is at a higher pressure than the air, which is why it spurts from a cut artery. The lower number, 80, is the pressure between beats, and it too is above air pressure.

why.correct: Blood vessels form a closed, stretchy system. Blood pressure depends partly on how much blood fills it. With a lower blood volume, the walls are stretched less and the pressure falls.
options: Correct. A smaller blood volume in the same vessels means less stretch and a lower pressure.
Losing blood, cells and fluid together, does not thicken what remains. Higher viscosity would raise resistance, not explain a pressure drop.
The surrounding air pressure is not changed by bleeding. Blood pressure readings are already relative to it.
The length of the vessels does not change with blood loss.

why.correct: Standing puts a column of blood more than a meter tall between your heart and your feet. Hydrostatic pressure rises with the depth of a fluid column, so pressure in foot vessels rises by roughly 90 mm Hg.
options: Gravity pulls blood toward the feet, not away, and the column above them raises the pressure.
Correct. The added hydrostatic pressure from the blood column raises foot-vessel pressure.
The heart's output is only part of the pressure. The weight of the blood column adds to it in the lowest parts of your body.
Atmospheric pressure acts on your whole body equally and does not change when you stand. The added pressure comes from the blood column.

why.correct: Heat moves down a temperature gradient, from warmer to cooler. Here the air is warmer than your skin, so heat moves into your skin.
options: That would be moving up the temperature gradient, from cooler (34 °C) to warmer (40 °C), which heat does not do on its own.
A 6 °C difference is a temperature gradient, so heat does move.
Heat moves in both directions only when there is no difference in temperature, and then the two cancel.
Correct. The air at 40 °C is warmer than skin at 34 °C, so heat moves into your skin.

why.correct: Most of blood's viscosity comes from its cells. More cells make blood more viscous, which raises resistance. With the same ΔP, F = ΔP / R falls.
options: Flow is the volume of blood moving per minute. More cells make blood thicker and harder to push, so flow falls.
The same ΔP drives less flow when resistance is higher. Flow depends on both.
Correct. Higher viscosity means higher resistance and less flow at the same pressure gradient.
Thick blood does not narrow the vessel. The rise in resistance comes from viscosity.

why.correct: Bulk flow is a whole fluid moving together, pushed by a pressure difference. Blood, inhaled air and IV fluid all qualify. Dye particles spreading through still water and heat passing into metal are driven by concentration and temperature gradients, with no pressure-driven flow of the fluid.
options: Bulk flow. The heart creates a pressure difference that moves the blood as a whole, with everything in it.
Not bulk flow. The water is still; individual dye particles spread down their own concentration gradient.
Bulk flow. The pressure in your lungs drops below atmospheric, and air moves in as a whole.
Bulk flow. The pressure at the bag end is higher than in the vein, so the fluid moves as a whole.
Not bulk flow. Heat moves down a temperature gradient; no fluid moves at all.

why.correct: Flow depends on the radius to the fourth power: 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9 ≈ 0.66. Resistance rises about 1.5-fold, so about two-thirds of the flow remains. A small narrowing costs a third of the flow.
options: This treats flow as directly proportional to radius. The fourth-power rule makes the loss much larger.
Correct. 0.9⁴ ≈ 0.66, so about 66% of the flow remains.
Half the flow would need the radius to shrink to about 0.84 of its original value, a 16% narrowing.
This confuses the size of the narrowing (10%) with the flow that remains.

why.correct: Steepness is the difference divided by the distance. The values are 2, 10, 0.5 and 1 mmol/L per mm, so 10 mmol/L across 1 mm is the steepest.
options: 20 ÷ 10 = 2 mmol/L per mm. The difference is larger, but it is spread over ten times the distance.
Correct. 10 ÷ 1 = 10 mmol/L per mm, the steepest of the four.
50 ÷ 100 = 0.5 mmol/L per mm. The largest difference, spread over the longest distance, gives the shallowest gradient.
5 ÷ 5 = 1 mmol/L per mm.

why.correct: The particles' random motion comes from heat and never stops. At equilibrium, as many particles cross any line one way as cross it the other way each second, so net diffusion is zero even though the particles keep moving.
options: The gradient is what disappears, not the motion. Without a gradient there is no net movement, but each particle still zigzags at random.
Dissolved dye particles do not settle out of solution. Their random motion keeps them spread through the water.
Correct. Net diffusion has stopped, but individual particles keep moving and crossing in both directions in equal numbers.
Stirring or warming speeds the motion, but particles move at random all the time because of heat, even in still water at room temperature.

why.correct: Each substance diffuses down its own gradient, whatever the others are doing. For a gas moving between air and blood, that gradient is in its pressure. Oxygen's pressure is higher in the air, so it moves into the blood; carbon dioxide's pressure is higher in the blood, so it moves into the air, at the same moment.
options: Correct. The two gases have opposite gradients, so they diffuse in opposite directions at the same time.
Gases do not take turns. Carbon dioxide has its own gradient from blood to air, and it diffuses down it at the same time oxygen diffuses the other way.
Carbon dioxide's pressure is higher in the blood, so its net diffusion is out of the blood. The speed of the blood does not set the direction.
The heart moves blood by bulk flow along the vessels, but crossing the thin barrier is diffusion, driven by each gas's own gradient.

why.correct: The glucose cannot cross, so it cannot even out by diffusion. Instead water crosses toward it by osmosis: side B gains volume and becomes more dilute, and side A loses volume.

variables.name: Volume of fluid on side A
variables.why: Side A now has fewer dissolved particles than side B, so water leaves side A by osmosis.

variables.name: Volume of fluid on side B
variables.why: Water follows solute: it moves into side B, where the glucose is, so the volume on side B rises.

variables.name: Amount of glucose on side A
variables.why: The membrane does not let glucose cross, so no glucose reaches side A.

variables.name: Osmolarity of side B, compared with just after the glucose was added
variables.why: The same glucose is now dissolved in more water, so side B becomes more dilute.

why.correct: Diffusion time grows with the square of the distance. Three times the distance gives 3 × 3 = 9 times the time: 3 seconds × 9 = 27 seconds.
options: This triples the time, treating diffusion time as proportional to distance. Time grows with the square of the distance, so it rises ninefold.
Correct. Three times the distance squared is nine times the time, and 3 × 9 = 27 seconds.
A thicker layer makes diffusion slower, not faster. This answer divides instead of multiplying.
This multiplies the time by 6 (twice the thickness factor). Squaring the factor of 3 gives 9, not 6.

why.correct: A larger surface area lets more particles cross each second, a bigger concentration difference makes the gradient steeper, and a thinner barrier shortens the diffusion distance. All three speed net diffusion.
options: Correct. Twice the area means twice as many places for particles to cross each second.
A thicker barrier lengthens the diffusion distance, which slows net diffusion.
Correct. A larger concentration difference is a steeper gradient, so more particles cross from the high side than cross back.
Larger particles move more slowly and spread more slowly, so this would slow diffusion rather than speed it.
Correct. A thinner barrier means a shorter distance, and diffusion is much faster over short distances.

why.correct: Fluid thickens the barrier, so oxygen has farther to travel. A longer diffusion distance slows net diffusion, so less oxygen enters his blood each minute even though the air is normal.
options: His body temperature is essentially unchanged, so this factor has not changed enough to explain the low oxygen.
An oxygen molecule is the same size whatever the disease. Particle size is fixed.
The question states that the air he breathes is normal, so the concentration on the air side has not changed.
Correct. The fluid layer lengthens the diffusion distance, and diffusion slows steeply as distance grows.

why.correct: Count particles. Sodium chloride gives 2 per unit: 100 × 2 = 200 mOsm/L on side A. Glucose gives 1: 150 mOsm/L on side B. Water follows solute, so it moves from B into A.
options: Millimoles of solute are not the measure that counts. Side A releases 200 mOsm/L of particles against 150 on side B, so water moves the other way.
Osmosis depends on the number of dissolved particles, not on what they are. The particle counts differ, so water moves.
Correct. Side A has 200 mOsm/L and side B 150 mOsm/L, so water moves from B toward A.
Solutes that cannot cross are exactly the ones that drive osmosis. Because neither crosses, the difference in particle count stays, and water moves.

why.correct: Sodium chloride gives 2 particles per unit: 150 × 2 = 300 mOsm/L. Glucose gives 1: 300 mOsm/L. With equal particle counts on both sides, water crosses equally in both directions and there is no net movement.
options: Millimoles of solute are not what counts. The sodium chloride splits into two ions, so both sides have the same particle count.
Osmosis depends on the number of particles, not on the kind. Salt has no special pull on water once the counts are equal.
Particle size does not matter for osmosis; particle number does. Both sides have the same number.
Correct. Both sides are 300 mOsm/L, so there is no difference to drive osmosis.

why.correct: Diluted blood means the fluid around her cells has fewer dissolved particles than the inside of the cells. Water follows solute, so it moves into the cells by osmosis and they swell. In the rigid skull, that raises pressure on the brain.
options: This is the direction for blood that has become more concentrated. Here the outside has become more dilute, so water moves in.
Correct. The inside of each cell now has more dissolved particles than the fluid around it, so water moves in.
The membranes around her cells hold most ions back, so the main change is water moving, not salt. And any change in particles would not leave the cells unchanged.
The skull protects the brain from knocks, but it does not stop osmosis across each cell's membrane. The rigid skull actually makes swelling more dangerous.

why.correct: X can cross, so it diffuses down its own gradient until it is equally concentrated on both sides. Then it no longer makes one side different from the other, so it drives no lasting water movement. Only particles the membrane holds back cause lasting osmosis.
options: That would happen only if the membrane held X back. Because X crosses, it spreads to both sides and the difference disappears.
Net diffusion moves X from high to low concentration until the two sides are equal, not until all of it is on the other side.
Correct. X evens out by diffusion, so there is no lasting difference in particle count and no lasting difference in water.
Diffusion is driven by the concentration gradient of X, not by a pressure difference, so X crosses even when the pressures are equal.

why.correct: Osmotic pressure is the pressure you would need to apply to a solution to stop water from entering it by osmosis. It measures how strongly the solution draws water in, and it rises with the number of dissolved particles the membrane holds back.
options: Correct. It is the pressure that would exactly balance the osmotic pull of the solution.
That describes hydrostatic pressure, the push a fluid exerts on its surroundings.
A pump supplies a pressure gradient for bulk flow. That has nothing to do with dissolved particles drawing water.
That is atmospheric pressure, the weight of the air above.

why.correct: The difference in osmolarity is 290 − 285 = 5 mOsm/L. Multiply by about 19 mm Hg per mOsm/L: 5 × 19 = 95 mm Hg. A tiny difference in particle count creates a large pressure.
options: This is the difference in osmolarity, in mOsm/L. It still has to be converted to mm Hg.
This is the pressure for a difference of 1 mOsm/L. The difference here is 5 mOsm/L.
Correct. 5 mOsm/L × 19 mm Hg per mOsm/L ≈ 95 mm Hg.
This is roughly the osmotic pressure of one whole solution against pure water (290 × 19). The question asks about the difference between the two solutions.

why.correct: The solute makes the right arm the side with more particles, so water moves in by osmosis and its level rises. The extra height adds hydrostatic pressure that pushes water back. When the push equals the osmotic pull, net movement stops. That balancing pressure is the solution's osmotic pressure.
Water follows solute. The cells hold dissolved particles their membranes keep in, and the water outside has none, so water moves into the cells by osmosis and they swell.
options: The membrane holds most of these particles back, so they cannot even out by diffusion. That is why water moves instead.
Correct. Water moves toward the side with more dissolved particles, which is the inside of the cells.
Water moves toward more dissolved particles, so here it moves in, not out. Moving out would shrink the cells.
No outside pressure is pushing. The water moves because of the difference in dissolved particles, which is osmosis, not bulk flow.

why.correct: Water moves toward the side with more dissolved particles, not fewer. The salty film outside has more particles than the inside of the cells, so water moves out of the cells, which is why they lose volume.
options: This step is right: the salt dissolves in the surface water and makes a concentrated solution.
This step is right: the membranes are semipermeable, open to water but not to most of the salt.
This is the error. Water follows solute, so it moves out of the cells into the salty film, not into the cells.
This step is right: losing water shrinks the cells, and the slices go limp.

why.correct: Diffusion is a random walk. Its time grows with the square of the distance, so a trip a million times longer takes about a million million times as long: roughly five years for a meter. Bulk flow of blood carries oxygen the long way instead.
options: Oxygen does diffuse through liquid; that is how it reaches your cells from the blood. It is just slow over long distances.
Oxygen falls steadily from lungs to tissues; the gradient does not reverse. The problem is the distance, not the direction.
Correct. Time grows with the square of distance, so diffusion that takes a fraction of a second over micrometers takes years over a meter.
Diffusion needs no membrane: dye spreads through a glass of water without one. A membrane can only limit it.

why.correct: The membrane holds the solute back, so the solute cannot even out. Water moves instead, toward the side with more dissolved particles, and that side's level rises.
options: The membrane does not let the solute cross, so the solute cannot even out by diffusion.
Correct. Water follows solute across the membrane, so the fluid level rises on the side with more dissolved particles.
This reverses the direction. Water moves toward more dissolved particles, not fewer.
The fluid level changed because water crossed the membrane. The weight of dissolved particles does not raise a fluid level.

why.correct: A semipermeable (selectively permeable) membrane is open to some substances and closed to others. The membrane around each of your cells lets water cross easily but holds back proteins and most ions.
options: Correct. Which substances it lets through is what makes it semipermeable.
Water crosses a semipermeable membrane in both directions all the time. Osmosis is the net difference between the two directions.
The prefix semi- means partly, as in partly permeable: open to some substances. It does not describe timing.
Many substances cross without any energy input, by diffusion. Being semipermeable describes what can cross, not how much energy it takes.

why.correct: Water follows solute. It leaves the cells toward the saltier outside, so the cells shrink, and the same particles in less water raise the osmolarity inside until it matches the outside.

variables.name: Volume of each cell
variables.why: The saltier outside has more dissolved particles than the inside of the cells, so water moves out by osmosis and the cells shrink.

variables.name: Osmolarity inside each cell
variables.why: The cells keep their dissolved particles but lose water, so the particles are packed into less water.

variables.name: Amount of dissolved particles inside each cell
variables.why: The membranes hold these particles back, so the count inside stays the same; only water leaves.

why.correct: Diffusion is dissolved or airborne particles spreading down their own concentration gradient by random motion. Carbon dioxide leaving a cell, coffee aroma in still air and oxygen entering the blood all fit. Pumped blood is bulk flow, and water crossing toward more solute is osmosis.
options: Correct. The cell makes carbon dioxide, so it is more concentrated inside, and it diffuses out down its gradient.
This is bulk flow: the whole fluid moves together, driven by the pressure gradient the heart creates.
Correct. With no air current, the aroma particles spread by their own random motion, from high to low concentration.
This is osmosis: net water movement across a semipermeable membrane toward the side with more dissolved particles.
Correct. Oxygen's pressure is higher in the air than in the arriving blood, so it diffuses into the blood.

why.correct: Voltage, also called potential difference, is always a difference between two points: how much electrical potential energy each unit of charge has at one point compared with the other. It exists only where charge is separated.
options: That describes electrical current, the flow of charge. A voltage can exist with no charge flowing at all.
Correct. Voltage is the potential difference between two points, measured in volts.
That describes electrical resistance, which opposes current.
Counting dissolved particles gives osmolarity, not voltage. A fluid full of ions can be perfectly neutral and have no voltage.

why.correct: 1 V = 1,000 mV, so multiply by 1,000: 0.065 × 1,000 = 65 mV. That is a typical size for the voltage across a cell's membrane.
options: This multiplies by 10 instead of 1,000.
This multiplies by 100 instead of 1,000.
This multiplies by 10,000 instead of 1,000.
Correct. 0.065 V × 1,000 mV per volt = 65 mV.

why.correct: Voltage exists only where charge is separated. Each beaker is neutral, with positive and negative charges balanced, so there is no difference in electrical potential between them.
options: Correct. No charge separation means no voltage, however many ions are present.
The number of ions does not create a voltage. Only an imbalance between two places does, and here both are neutral.
Osmolarity counts dissolved particles and matters for water movement. It is not a voltage.
Random motion of ions in a neutral fluid produces no voltage. A voltage needs separated charge, not moving charge.

why.correct: Chloride carries negative charge, so bringing it in makes the inside more negative. By convention, current points the way positive charge moves, and bringing negative charge in has the same effect as taking positive charge out, so the current is outward.
options: Chloride is negative, so it makes the inside more negative, not more positive.
The inside does become more negative, but current direction follows positive charge. Negative ions moving in make an outward current.
Correct. Negative charge entering makes the inside more negative, which counts as an outward current.
The current is indeed outward, but chloride is negative, so it makes the inside more negative, not more positive.

why.correct: Sodium's concentration gradient pushes it inward, and as a positive ion it is attracted to the negative inside. Both parts of its electrochemical gradient point inward, so it rushes in.
options: A negative inside attracts positive ions such as sodium; it does not push them away.
Correct. The chemical and electrical pushes add together, giving a strong inward electrochemical gradient.
The two gradients would cancel only if they pointed in opposite directions. For sodium, both point inward.
Sodium is charged, so the voltage acts on it too. Both pushes act, and they add together.

why.correct: Potassium is higher inside, so its concentration gradient pushes it out. It is a positive ion, so the negative inside attracts it, pulling it in. The two pushes oppose each other, and the net push is the difference between them.
options: The voltage does not push potassium out. A negative inside attracts positive ions.
The concentration gradient does not push potassium in; there is more potassium inside than outside.
Correct. The chemical push is outward and the electrical pull is inward, so they partly cancel.
This reverses both directions. Potassium moves from high to low concentration (outward), and the negative inside attracts it (inward).

why.correct: A voltage pushes only charged particles. Glucose has no net charge, so it follows its concentration gradient alone, from higher (outside) to lower (inside).
options: A voltage acts only on charged particles. Glucose carries no net charge, so the voltage does not pull it.
A voltage cannot push an uncharged particle in either direction.
Only ions have an electrochemical gradient. For an uncharged particle, the electrical part is zero.
Correct. With no charge, glucose feels only its concentration gradient, which points inward here.

why.correct: Current equals voltage divided by resistance. With the voltage fixed, doubling the resistance halves the current, exactly as doubling the resistance of a tube halves fluid flow.

variables.name: Electrical resistance of the path
variables.why: Fewer open routes make it harder for ions to cross, so resistance rises; the question says it doubles.

variables.name: Voltage across the membrane
variables.why: The question holds the voltage constant.

variables.name: Ion current
variables.why: I = V / R. The same voltage divided by twice the resistance gives half the current.

why.correct: I = V / R = 6 V ÷ 2,000 Ω = 0.003 A. Since 1 A = 1,000 mA, that is 3 mA.
options: Correct. 6 ÷ 2,000 = 0.003 A, which is 3 mA.
This multiplies voltage by resistance instead of dividing. Current is voltage divided by resistance.
This misplaces the decimal point. 6 ÷ 2,000 = 0.003 A, and 0.003 A is 3 mA, not 0.3 mA.
This divides resistance by voltage (2,000 ÷ 6 ≈ 333) instead of voltage by resistance.

why.correct: A very thin layer of separated charge, a tiny fraction of the ions, lines the two faces of the membrane. Setting it up takes energy, which is stored. The rest of the fluid on each side is neutral, and the voltage exists whether or not anything is flowing.
options: Correct. Far less than one ion in a thousand is part of the separated layer.
Away from the membrane, the fluid inside is almost perfectly neutral. The excess negative charge is only a thin layer at the membrane.
Correct. Opposite charges attract, so pulling them apart takes energy, which is stored like the energy in a stretched spring.
Correct. The separated charges line the inner and outer faces of the membrane.
Voltage is a stored push. Like a battery on a shelf, a membrane has a voltage even when no current flows.

why.correct: Energy builds the concentration differences. Leaking positive ions separate charge, which creates a voltage. When a new route opens, an ion current flows, and because the moving ions carry charge, the voltage changes.
Potassium ions are positive. As they leave, they carry positive charge out and leave more negative charge behind, so the charge separation grows and the inside becomes more negative.
options: No negative ions need to move. The change comes from positive charge leaving.
Correct. Each potassium ion that leaves takes positive charge out, increasing the separation.
A tiny number of ions changes the voltage a lot, so the concentration inside barely changes at all.
If the pushes balanced exactly, there would be no net movement and no change in voltage. The chain says potassium flows out.

why.correct: The electrochemical gradient is the concentration part plus the electrical part. With no concentration difference, the electrical part still acts, so the ion has an inward electrochemical gradient and moves in when a route opens.
options: This step is right: equal concentrations mean no concentration gradient.
This step is right: the ion is positive, and the inside is negative.
This step is right: a negative inside attracts a positive ion.
This is the error. The electrical gradient alone is enough to move a charged particle, so the ion moves inward.

why.correct: A concentration gradient depends on the difference between the two sides. More potassium outside, with the same amount inside, shrinks that difference, so the outward chemical push weakens. Less positive charge leaves, and the voltage across the membrane becomes smaller.
options: The push depends on the difference between inside and outside, not the total amount. Raising the outside level shrinks the difference.
The push depends on both sides. Changing the outside changes the difference even though the inside is the same.
The question says potassium is still more concentrated inside, so the chemical push still points outward, just more weakly.
Correct. A smaller difference means a gentler gradient and a weaker outward push.

why.correct: I = V / R. The voltage is fixed at 120 V. Salty water on the skin lowers its resistance, so a larger current flows through the body, and current is what disturbs cells.
options: The supply voltage is set by the wiring, not by the person touching it. It is 120 V both times.
The thin film of water does not store a meaningful charge. The danger comes from more current flowing from the supply.
Correct. Same voltage, less resistance, more current.
Wet skin lowers resistance rather than raising it, and a higher resistance would reduce the current, not trap it.

why.correct: The voltage comes from a very thin layer of separated charge. Moving a tiny number of ions changes that layer a great deal, so the voltage changes a lot while the total amount of each ion inside and outside hardly changes.
options: Nothing replaces the ions instantly. The concentrations stay steady because so few ions are needed to change the voltage.
A voltage changes only when the charge separation changes, which means charges must move.
Correct. A few ions make a big change in charge separation but a negligible change in concentration.
Uncharged particles carry no charge, so their movement cannot change a voltage.

why.correct: In your body, the charge carriers are ions dissolved in water, such as sodium, potassium, calcium and chloride. Their movement is an ion current.
options: Correct. Your body's currents are ion currents.
Wires carry current as electrons, but your tissues have no wires. Charged ions in the fluids carry the current.
Water molecules carry no net charge, so their movement is not an electrical current.
Heat is the kinetic energy of moving particles, not a flow of charge.

why.correct: More of the ion is inside, so its concentration gradient pushes it out. It is positive and the inside is positive, so like charges repel and the voltage also pushes it out. Both parts point outward.
options: Correct. The concentration gradient and the electrical repulsion both push the ion out.
Like charges repel. A positive inside pushes positive ions away, not toward it.
Both pushes point outward, so no comparison is needed; the ion is pushed out whatever their sizes.
The pushes would cancel only if they pointed in opposite directions. Here both point out.

why.correct: The phosphate heads are polar and hydrophilic, so they face the water: the outer sheet's heads face the extracellular fluid and the inner sheet's heads face the cytoplasm.
options: The fatty acid tails are hydrophobic. They point inward and meet in the middle, forming the oily core, away from water.
Correct. The hydrophilic heads face the water on both sides of the membrane.
Cholesterol sits between phospholipids in the bilayer, but it is a separate molecule, not bonded to the tails.
Sugar chains are attached to some proteins and lipids on the outer surface only, and never to the hydrophobic tails.

why.correct: Oxygen is small and nonpolar, so it dissolves in the bilayer's hydrophobic core and crosses without any protein.
options: Sodium ions carry a charge and hold a shell of water molecules around them. Moving them into the oily core costs a great deal of energy, so the bare bilayer almost blocks them.
Glucose is large and polar. It barely crosses a bare bilayer; cells take it in through specific transport proteins.
Correct. Oxygen is small and nonpolar, so it passes through the oily core on its own.
Potassium ions are charged, like sodium ions, so the hydrophobic core almost blocks them.

why.correct: Membrane proteins transport specific substances, act as enzymes, bind signals, anchor the cell and, as glycoproteins, carry identity markers.
options: Correct. Transport proteins give specific ions and molecules a way across the bilayer.
The oily core is made by the fatty acid tails of the phospholipids, not by proteins.
Correct. Some membrane proteins are enzymes that work right at the cell surface.
Correct. Glycoproteins carry sugar chains that are part of the glycocalyx and mark cell identity.
Genetic instructions are stored in the nucleus, not in the plasma membrane.

why.correct: Red blood cells hold about 25 times more potassium than plasma does. When their membranes tear, that potassium pours into the plasma in the tube, so the lab measures a falsely high value. The pink color is from the contents of the burst cells.
options: The fresh sample was normal, so his kidneys are handling potassium fine. The problem was in the tube, not in him.
Correct. Burst red cells released their potassium-rich cytoplasm into the plasma in the tube.
Potassium moving into cells would lower plasma potassium, not raise it.
Platelets do not release sodium in amounts that could do this, and lab machines measure sodium and potassium separately.

why.correct: The glycocalyx (glyco- = sugar, calyx = husk) is the coat of sugar chains attached to proteins and lipids on the outer surface of the plasma membrane.
options: Correct. The glycocalyx is the sugar coat on the outside of the cell.
There is no fat layer under the membrane. The only lipid in the membrane is in the bilayer itself.
There is a protein framework under the membrane, but it is not the glycocalyx, and the glycocalyx is on the outside, never the inside.
Human cells have one plasma membrane, a single bilayer. The glycocalyx is sugar chains, not another bilayer.

why.correct: This is an integral protein. Its hydrophobic amino acids sit inside the oily core of the bilayer, so it comes out only when the bilayer itself is broken apart.
options: Sugar chains are attached to proteins, but they do not anchor a protein into the membrane. Its hydrophobic region does that.
A protein sitting loosely on a surface is a peripheral protein. Those are the ones that wash off with salt water.
Correct. An integral protein's hydrophobic region is held in the bilayer's core.
Membrane proteins are made of amino acids like every protein. What matters is which of those amino acids are hydrophobic.

why.correct: From outside in: the interstitial fluid bathes the cell; the glycocalyx is the sugar coat on the outer face; then come the hydrophilic heads of the outer sheet, the hydrophobic tails of both sheets meeting in the middle, the heads of the inner sheet, and finally the cytoplasm.
Glucose leaves the capillary into the interstitial fluid that bathes the cell, then crosses the plasma membrane into the cytoplasm.
options: Correct. Interstitial fluid lies between the capillary and the cells it supplies.
Intracellular fluid is inside the cell. Glucose reaches it only after crossing the plasma membrane, so it cannot come before the membrane.
Red blood cells stay in the blood. Their glycocalyx is not on the path from plasma to a tissue cell.
The nucleus is deep inside the cell, past the cytoplasm, not between the blood and the cell.

why.correct: Hydrophobic tails do not mix with water. They are excluded from it, which is exactly why they end up hidden in the middle of the bilayer.
options: This step is right. A bilayer forms when phospholipids are in water, as they are in your body.
This step is right. The polar heads are hydrophilic and interact with water.
This is the error. The tails are hydrophobic, so they are kept away from water, not drawn toward it.
This step is right. Tail to tail is the arrangement that shields every tail from water.
This step is right. The hydrophobic core is the barrier to charged particles.

why.correct: High sodium and low potassium is the pattern of extracellular fluid. Interstitial fluid is extracellular fluid.
options: Red cell cytoplasm is intracellular fluid. It is high in potassium and low in sodium, the reverse of this sample.
Correct. High sodium with low potassium marks extracellular fluid, and interstitial fluid is part of it.
Fluid inside a white blood cell is intracellular fluid, which has high potassium and low sodium.
Intracellular fluid in general has about 140 mmol/L potassium and only 10 to 15 mmol/L sodium.

why.correct: Extracellular fluid is all fluid outside cells. Its two main parts are interstitial fluid, which bathes the cells, and plasma, the fluid part of blood.
options: Correct. Plasma is outside the blood cells, so it is extracellular fluid.
Correct. Interstitial fluid fills the spaces between cells and is most of the extracellular fluid.
The fluid of the cytoplasm is intracellular fluid.
A red blood cell is a cell, so the fluid inside it is intracellular, even though the cell itself floats in plasma.
The nucleus is inside the cell, so its fluid is intracellular.

why.correct: Cholesterol wedges between phospholipids. At body temperature it restrains the tails, making the membrane less fluid and less leaky; at low temperature it stops the tails packing into a stiff sheet. The membrane stays about equally fluid over a range of temperatures.
options: Cholesterol is itself mostly nonpolar and makes the core less leaky, not more open to ions.
The sugar coat is the glycocalyx, made of sugar chains on proteins and lipids. Cholesterol is not part of it.
Glucose crosses through specific transport proteins, not through cholesterol.
Correct. Cholesterol buffers membrane fluidity in both directions.

why.correct: The membrane is fluid: each phospholipid moves sideways and swaps places with its neighbors millions of times a second. That is the "fluid" in the fluid mosaic model.
options: This is true, but it supports the classmate's idea, since it describes a movement that almost never happens. It does not show that phospholipids move.
This is true, but it is about where sugars are, not about whether phospholipids move.
This is true, but it describes how firmly proteins are anchored in the bilayer, not whether lipids move.
Correct. Sideways drift within a sheet shows that phospholipids do not stay in one spot.

why.correct: Platelets gather at a break in a blood vessel and help seal it. With too few platelets, small cuts keep bleeding longer.
options: Correct. Platelets help seal breaks in blood vessels, so too few of them means slow-stopping bleeding.
Defending against infection is the job of white blood cells, and her white cell count is normal.
Oxygen is carried by red blood cells, and her red cell count is normal.
A low platelet count does not raise plasma potassium. Burst red cells in a sample can, but that is a different problem.

why.correct: Red blood cells carry oxygen from the lungs to the tissues. They push out their nucleus as they mature.
options: White blood cells keep their nucleus and defend against infection; they do not carry oxygen.
Platelets have no nucleus, but they are cell fragments that help seal broken vessels, not oxygen carriers.
Correct. Mature red blood cells have no nucleus and carry oxygen.
Plasma is the fluid part of blood, not a cell. It carries only a little dissolved oxygen compared with red blood cells.

why.correct: A living membrane holds transport proteins, each for one substance or a small family of them, and the cell can add or remove them. Adding proteins that carry sodium opens a path for sodium. That control is what makes the membrane selectively permeable; holes punched in plastic cannot change.
options: Phospholipids drift sideways but stay packed side by side. The bilayer does not open gaps for ions.
The oily core blocks charged particles such as sodium ions, whatever signal arrives. Ions cross through proteins.
Correct. By adding transport proteins, the cell changes what crosses its membrane.
The glycocalyx is sugar chains on the outer face. It does not carry sodium across the membrane.

why.correct: Burst cells release their intracellular fluid into the plasma in the tube, which gives a falsely high potassium result while the patient is unchanged.

variables.name: Potassium measured in the sample's plasma
variables.why: The red cells' cytoplasm is potassium-rich. Their torn membranes no longer separate it from the plasma, so potassium spills into the plasma.

variables.name: Potassium in the patient's own bloodstream
variables.why: The cells burst in the tube after it left the patient. Nothing changed in the patient's body.

variables.name: Number of intact red blood cells in the tube
variables.why: Each cell whose membrane tears is no longer an intact cell, so the count of whole red cells falls.

why.correct: A mitochondrion has a smooth outer membrane and a folded inner membrane (cristae). The ATP-making protein complexes sit on that inner membrane.
options: The Golgi is a stack of flattened sacs with single membranes. It modifies and sorts proteins; it does not make ATP.
Correct. The mitochondrion's folded inner membrane holds the ATP-making machinery.
The smooth ER is a network of single-membrane tubes. It makes lipids and breaks down some drugs.
A lysosome is a single-membrane sac of digestive enzymes.

why.correct: Rough ER builds and folds proteins for export, and the Golgi packages them into vesicles bound for the surface. A cell full of both is a protein exporter, like the pancreas cells that make digestive enzymes.
options: Correct. Rough ER plus a large Golgi plus vesicles at the surface is the equipment of a protein-exporting cell.
Steroids are lipids made in the smooth ER. A steroid-making cell would be full of smooth ER, not rough ER.
Absorbing cells are marked by a brush border of microvilli, which this description does not mention.
Moving fluid across a surface is the job of cilia, which this description does not mention.

why.correct: Cilia and flagella have a core of nine microtubule pairs around two central ones, and each centriole is nine sets of three microtubules. Microvilli have an actin core, and intermediate filaments are their own kind of fiber.
options: Correct. A cilium's core is microtubules arranged as nine pairs around two.
Correct. A flagellum has the same microtubule core as a cilium, only longer.
Correct. Each centriole is a short cylinder of nine sets of three microtubules.
Microvilli have a core of actin microfilaments, which is why they do not beat.
Intermediate filaments are a separate, rope-like fiber of the cytoskeleton, not microtubules.

why.correct: Motor proteins such as kinesin and dynein carry vesicles and organelles by walking along microtubules. Without microtubules, those tracks are gone.
options: The brush border is made of microvilli, which have an actin core, not microtubules.
Correct. Microtubules are the tracks that motor proteins use to carry vesicles.
Catalase breaks down hydrogen peroxide inside peroxisomes. That does not depend on microtubule tracks.
Fuel oxidation happens on and inside the mitochondrion's inner membrane, not on microtubules.
