options: Correct. Between leaving the cell and entering a capillary, the hormone crosses the interstitial fluid by diffusion.
The pituitary gland is endocrine, so it has no duct. Ducts belong to exocrine glands.
Release onto a surface is what an exocrine gland does. An endocrine product heads for the blood.
A cell responding to its own product is autocrine signaling. That would not lead on to the hormone entering a capillary and traveling in the blood.

why.correct: An exocrine product stays in the duct system and is delivered to a surface. Entering capillaries is the route of an endocrine product.
options: This step is correct. The secretory portion of an alveolar gland is its rounded sacs.
This step is correct. Exocytosis on the apical side empties the product into the lumen of the sac.
This is the wrong step. An exocrine product does not enter the blood; it flows from the sac into the duct system.
This step is correct. In a compound gland, the branching ducts join like tree branches into one main duct.
This step is correct. The duct delivers the product to a surface, here the inside of the gut.

why.correct: Exocrine and endocrine describe the route, not the chemical. A duct to a surface means exocrine; release into interstitial fluid and then blood means endocrine. The student's rule fails whenever a product breaks the pattern, and it cannot classify mucus at all.
options: Enzymes are proteins, and so are many hormones. Knowing the product is a protein does not tell you which way it leaves.
Both exocrine and endocrine cells can store their product in secretory vesicles and release it by exocytosis.
Correct. Tracing where the product goes is the test that defines the two kinds of gland.
Size separates a goblet cell from larger exocrine glands, but it does not separate exocrine from endocrine: both kinds include many-celled glands.

why.correct: A serous gland (ser/o = watery fluid) releases a thin, watery fluid that is often rich in enzymes. Its cells hold many protein-filled vesicles.
options: A mucous gland releases thick, sticky mucus, made thick by large glycoproteins called mucins. This fluid is thin and watery.
Correct. Thin, watery, enzyme-rich fluid from protein-packed cells marks a serous gland.
Holocrine names how a cell releases its product (by breaking apart), not what the product is. Nothing here says the cells break apart.
A ductless gland is an endocrine gland. The question describes an exocrine gland.

why.correct: In the milk-making gland of the breast, fat droplets leave from the apical end of the cell wrapped in a piece of its plasma membrane: true apocrine release. Some exams instead name the "apocrine" sweat-producing glands of the armpit, but electron microscope studies show those release mainly by exocytosis, so their name is historical.
options: A goblet cell releases mucus by exocytosis and stays whole. That is merocrine secretion.
The oil glands of the skin are holocrine: whole cells fill with product and break apart.
The thyroid gland is endocrine. The three mode names describe exocrine glands, and its hormone release is not apocrine.
Correct. Fat droplets pinching off in a wrap of plasma membrane is the clearest example of apocrine release.

why.correct: Merocrine release is exocytosis. Vesicles empty their contents, and the cell loses nothing else, so it keeps working.
options: Correct. A merocrine cell releases only the vesicle contents and survives unchanged.
Losing the apical part of the cell with the product is apocrine secretion.
Breaking apart so the whole cell becomes the product is holocrine secretion.
A merocrine cell survives, so there is nothing to replace. Steady replacement by dividing stem cells is what holocrine glands need.

why.correct: An endocrine product enters the blood and can act far away. A chemical that diffuses only to nearby cells and acts on them is a paracrine signal. Lacking a duct does not by itself make cells an endocrine gland; the product must also reach the blood.
options: Endocrine signaling needs the messenger to enter the blood. This chemical never does, so the cells are not acting as an endocrine gland.
Correct. Local diffusion to neighboring cells without entering the blood is paracrine signaling.
Exocrine secretion delivers a product through a duct onto a surface. This chemical acts on neighboring cells inside the tissue.
Holocrine describes a cell breaking apart to release its product. Nothing here says the cells break apart, and the question is about where the chemical acts.

why.correct: Apo- means off or away. In apocrine secretion the apical end of the cell, holding the product, pinches off inside a wrap of plasma membrane, and the rest of the cell repairs itself.
options: Vesicle fusion with the cell left whole is merocrine secretion.
Correct. Losing the product-filled apical part of the cell is apocrine secretion.
A whole cell breaking apart is holocrine secretion.
Diffusion into capillaries describes the route of an endocrine product, not a mode of secretion.

why.correct: The synovial membrane is a connective tissue membrane. It is areolar connective tissue with a lining layer of cells facing the joint space, but no epithelium.
options: A mucous membrane is an epithelial membrane: an epithelium over the lamina propria.
A serous membrane is an epithelial membrane: simple squamous mesothelium over thin connective tissue.
Correct. The synovial membrane is the one connective tissue membrane.
The cutaneous membrane (skin) has an epithelium: the keratinized stratified squamous epidermis.

why.correct: A lining of a tract open to the outside, with epithelium over a lamina propria of loose connective tissue, is a mucous membrane (mucosa). The goblet cells keep it coated with mucus.
options: A serous membrane lines a closed cavity and has simple squamous epithelium, not columnar epithelium with goblet cells.
The cutaneous membrane is the skin, whose surface is keratinized stratified squamous epithelium.
A synovial membrane has no epithelium and lines the space inside a movable joint.
Correct. Epithelium plus lamina propria, lining a tube open to the outside, is a mucosa.

why.correct: The outer covering of the stomach is the visceral peritoneum, a serous membrane. Its simple squamous mesothelium releases thin serous fluid into the closed peritoneal cavity, which lets organs slide with little friction.
options: The stomach's inner lining is a mucous membrane, but this sample is from its outer surface, facing the closed abdominal cavity.
Correct. A single layer of flat cells lining a closed cavity is a serous membrane, and it releases serous fluid.
Synovial membranes line the spaces inside movable joints, not the abdominal cavity.
A mucous membrane lines a tract open to the outside and is not simple squamous. This membrane faces a closed cavity.

why.correct: An epithelial membrane is an epithelium attached to connective tissue. The mucous, serous and cutaneous membranes all fit.
options: Epithelial membrane: epithelium over the lamina propria.
Epithelial membrane: mesothelium over thin connective tissue.
Epithelial membrane: the epidermis over the dermis.
Not an epithelial membrane. The synovial membrane is made of connective tissue alone.
Not a tissue membrane at all. A plasma membrane is the lipid bilayer around a single cell.

why.correct: Histamine opens gaps between the endothelial cells of capillaries and the smallest veins. Water and proteins from plasma leak into the interstitial fluid, and the tissue swells.
options: Inflammation causes vasodilation, not vasoconstriction. Narrower arteries would bring less blood and would not cause swelling.
Collagen is laid down days later during repair. It does not explain swelling within an hour.
Correct. Fluid leaking out of leaky vessels into the interstitial fluid is what makes the tissue swell.
Mast cells release histamine within minutes; they do not multiply to cause swelling. The swelling comes from fluid, not extra cells.

variables.name: Amount of histamine released by mast cells
variables.why: The drug acts on the receptor proteins of the target cells, not on the mast cells, so release is unchanged.

variables.name: Blood flow into the area
variables.why: With its receptor proteins blocked, histamine causes less vasodilation of the small arteries, so less blood flows in and the area is less red and warm.

variables.name: Swelling
variables.why: Histamine can no longer make capillaries and the smallest veins as leaky, so less fluid leaks into the interstitial fluid.

why.correct: Bleeding and clotting come first. Chemical messengers then start inflammation, whose vessel changes bring in white blood cells. Macrophages clear the debris, which lets new capillaries and fibroblasts move in. The final outcome is regeneration where cells can divide and the framework survives, and fibrosis where it does not.

Cardiac muscle regenerates very little because its cells rarely divide. Fibroblasts filled the gap with collagen (fibrosis). Scar tissue holds the wall together but cannot contract, so that region stays still.
options: Correct. The muscle cells of the heart rarely divide, so the heart repairs by fibrosis, and scar tissue does not contract.
Cardiac muscle regenerates very little. Months later, the region is scar, not immature muscle.
Inflammation after an injury like this settles within weeks. A thin, still wall months later reflects scar tissue.
Cells that die from lost blood supply die by necrosis, not apoptosis, and the gap they leave is filled by repair.

why.correct: Regeneration needs cells of the lost type that can divide. Mature liver cells can re-enter the cell cycle and multiply; the heart's muscle cells rarely do, so the heart fills the gap with scar tissue.
options: Correct. Whether the working cells can divide is the main factor that decides regeneration or fibrosis.
The heart has a very rich blood supply too. Blood supply alone does not decide whether a tissue regenerates.
The heart does have fibroblasts; they are what make the scar. Having fibroblasts favors fibrosis, not regeneration.
Liver injury does cause inflammation. Inflammation starts repair in both organs; the outcome differs because of cell division.

why.correct: Swelling, membrane rupture, many neighboring cells dying together, and inflammation around them are the marks of necrosis, cell death caused by injury.
options: In apoptosis the cell shrinks and breaks into sealed pieces, and no inflammation follows.
Mitosis is cell division, not cell death.
Regeneration replaces lost cells; it is not a way cells die.
Correct. Swollen, ruptured cells with inflammation around them point to necrosis.

why.correct: In apoptosis the cell breaks into small membrane-wrapped pieces, and macrophages engulf them before anything spills. In necrosis the membrane ruptures and the spilled contents act as danger signals that start inflammation.
options: Histamine comes mainly from mast cells, and extra histamine would promote inflammation, not prevent it.
Apoptosis happens throughout the body, including in tissues with a rich blood supply, such as the gut lining.
Correct. The apoptotic cell breaks into membrane-wrapped pieces that macrophages engulf before anything spills, so there are no danger signals to start inflammation.
This describes apoptosis, not necrosis. Necrotic cells swell and burst.

why.correct: Histamine causes vasodilation, not vasoconstriction. Wider small arteries bring in more warm blood, which is why an inflamed area is red and warm.
options: This step is correct. Mast cells hold histamine in granules and release it when tissue is injured.
This is the wrong step. Vasoconstriction would reduce blood flow and make the area pale and cool, the opposite of what you see.
This step is correct. That leakiness is what lets fluid and proteins from the plasma out of the vessels.
This step is correct. Fluid leaking into the interstitial fluid causes the swelling.
This step is correct. That is where the pain of inflammation comes from.

why.correct: Histamine causes vasodilation of the small arteries that feed the injured area. Wider vessels carry more warm blood in, causing redness and heat.
options: Correct. Vasodilation is the step between histamine release and increased blood flow.
Collagen deposition is a later repair step and does not change blood flow.
Clotted capillaries would reduce blood flow, not increase it.
Macrophages clear debris, but that does not explain the increased blood flow.

why.correct: Epidermis regenerates well, but it needs an intact framework to rebuild the right shape. In a shallow scrape the deeper connective tissue survives, so stem cells regrow normal skin. In a deep cut the framework is destroyed and collagen fills the gap as scar tissue.
options: A bigger clot does not make regeneration more likely. The deep cut destroys the framework, so it is the one that scars.
Correct. Surviving framework plus dividing stem cells in the epidermis allows regeneration without a scar.
Both involve skin, but depth decides the outcome. The deep cut loses its framework and scars.
Shallow injuries of the epidermis regenerate without scarring. Fibrosis fills only deeper gaps.

why.correct: The parenchyma is the organ's working cells, the ones that do its job. Regeneration replaces parenchyma with parenchyma; fibrosis replaces it with connective tissue.
options: The connective tissue framework supports the parenchyma and carries its blood vessels, but it is not the parenchyma.
A serous covering is a membrane on the outside of some organs, not their working cells.
Correct. The parenchyma is the functional cells of an organ.
Scar tissue replaces lost parenchyma; it is not parenchyma.

why.correct: The space inside a movable joint such as the knee is lined by a synovial membrane. It is a connective tissue membrane, and its lining cells release the thick, slippery joint fluid.
options: Serous membranes line the closed body cavities, such as the pleural and peritoneal cavities, not joint spaces.
Mucous membranes line tracts open to the outside of the body. The space inside the knee is sealed.
Correct. A synovial membrane, made of connective tissue, lines the joint and releases its fluid.
The skin covers the knee from outside. It does not line the joint space or release joint fluid.

why.correct: The cutaneous membrane is the only dry membrane. Its outer cells are dead and filled with keratin, and it releases no mucus or serous fluid onto its surface.
options: Correct. A dry, keratinized surface is what sets the skin apart.
All three epithelial membranes rest on connective tissue, so this does not set the skin apart.
Every tissue membrane covers or lines something, so this does not distinguish the skin.
The mucosa of the mouth is also stratified, so having several cell layers is not unique to the skin.

variables.name: Amount of collagen in the liver
variables.why: With each round of injury, fibroblasts lay down more collagen, and fibrosis builds up faster than it is removed.

variables.name: Number of working liver cells (parenchyma)
variables.why: Scar tissue gradually replaces working cells, and the scar distorts the framework that regeneration needs.

variables.name: The liver's ability to do its jobs
variables.why: Scar tissue holds the organ together but does not do the work of the lost liver cells, so function falls as the scar grows.

why.correct: The set point is the target value, such as about 37 °C for body temperature. It sits inside the normal range, and negative feedback pulls the variable back toward it.
options: The top of the normal range is not the set point. The set point sits inside the range, and the variable swings above and below it.
Correct. The set point is the value the control center compares the input with.
A positive feedback loop ends with an outside event, such as delivery of a baby. That is not what a set point means.
A set point is a value, not a location. Sensory receptors detect the variable; the control center compares it with the set point.

why.correct: After the stimulus changes the regulated variable, the sensory receptor (sensor) detects it and sends information along the afferent pathway (toward) to the control center. The control center compares it with the set point and sends commands along the efferent pathway (away) to the effector, which produces the response.
The effector is the tissue that carries out the command. Here the smooth muscle in the vessel walls contracts, causing vasoconstriction.
options: The cold air causes the stimulus, the drop in temperature. It is not part of the body's loop.
Nerves carrying commands from the brain are the efferent pathway, not the effector.
Correct. The smooth muscle does the work that changes the variable, so it is the effector.
The brain region that compares temperature with the set point is the control center.

why.correct: The afferent pathway (af- = toward) carries information from the sensory receptor toward the control center. Sensory nerves running from the skin to the brain do exactly that.
options: The efferent pathway carries commands away from the control center to the effector. These nerves carry information toward it.
The control center is where input is compared with the set point: here, a region of the brain. The nerves only carry the information there.
Correct. Signals arriving at the control center travel on the afferent pathway.
An effector carries out a response. These nerves do not change body temperature themselves.

variables.name: Diameter of the blood vessels in your skin
variables.why: The control center sends signals that relax the smooth muscle of skin blood vessels, so they dilate (vasodilation).

variables.name: Amount of sweat released onto your skin
variables.why: The control center signals the sweat glands to release sweat; as it evaporates, it carries heat away.

variables.name: Heat lost from your skin to the air
variables.why: More warm blood near the surface and more evaporating sweat both increase heat loss, which opposes the rise in temperature.

variables.name: Blood flow to the skin
variables.why: With the efferent pathway to the vessels broken, the command to constrict never arrives, so the skin vessels stay wider than in an intact person.

variables.name: Heat lost through the skin
variables.why: More warm blood near the cold surface loses more heat to the air.

variables.name: Body temperature after an hour
variables.why: Heat loss is not reduced, so body temperature falls further below the set point than it would in a person with an intact loop.

why.correct: Each response (more platelets sticking) strengthens the stimulus that caused it (more of the chemicals). A response that amplifies its own stimulus is positive feedback. The loop ends only when the tear is sealed.
options: Correct. The response strengthens the stimulus, so the change grows until an outside event, sealing the tear, stops it.
Negative feedback would oppose the change and reduce platelet sticking. Here each step increases it.
Mass balance compares inputs and outputs of a substance. It does not describe a loop in which a response amplifies itself.
Feedforward control starts a response before a variable changes. Here the response follows and strengthens an existing change.

why.correct: Labor contractions are driven by positive feedback: stretch of the lower opening of the uterus causes hormone release, which strengthens contractions, which cause more stretch. A positive loop cannot stop itself. Delivery is an outside event that removes the stretch, so the stimulus disappears and the loop ends.
options: The contractions grew stronger, not steadier, which is positive feedback. There is no set point that they are returned to.
Muscle does not simply run out of ATP within minutes of delivery. The loop stops because its stimulus is gone.
Correct. Removing the stretch removes the stimulus, and a positive loop ends when its stimulus is removed from outside.
Positive feedback does not settle at a set point. The loop ends because something outside it, delivery, removes the stimulus.

why.correct: "Negative" means the response opposes the stimulus, not that it lowers the variable. The stimulus was a fall in pH; the response raises it. Opposing the change back toward the set point is negative feedback.
options: Positive feedback would push the pH further in the direction it was already moving, lower still. Here the response raises it, which opposes the change.
Correct. A fall triggered a rise: the response opposes the change, which is negative feedback. "Negative" means opposing, not lowering.
Mass balance compares the input and output of a substance. It describes what disturbs a variable, not the loop that corrects it.
A response that pulls the variable back toward its set point is a feedback loop at work. Moving outside the normal range is the stimulus that starts it.

why.correct: Negative feedback opposes the change. That pulls the variable back toward the set point, whichever direction it moved, and the loop switches itself off as the stimulus shrinks.
options: True. Opposing the stimulus is the defining feature of negative feedback.
True. Opposing the change returns the variable toward its set point.
True. If the variable falls, the opposing response raises it, as when shivering warms a cold body.
False. Needing an outside event to stop is a feature of positive feedback. Negative feedback stops itself as the stimulus shrinks.
False. A response that enlarges the original change is positive feedback.

why.correct: Mass balance: change = input − output = 2.8 L − 2.4 L = +0.4 L per day. With input greater than output every day, body water builds up.
options: The amount stays the same only if input equals output. Here input is larger by 0.4 liters a day.
Body water falls only when output exceeds input. Here output is smaller.
Correct. Input exceeds output, so water accumulates, about 0.4 liters a day.
Nothing in the numbers changes during the week. As long as input exceeds output, water keeps accumulating.

why.correct: Change per day = input − output = 200 − 170 = +30 mmol. Over four days: 30 × 4 = +120 mmol.
options: The sign is wrong. Input is larger than output, so sodium builds up rather than falling.
30 mmol is the change for one day. Multiply by four days.
Correct. +30 mmol per day for four days is +120 mmol.
800 mmol is the total input over four days. The change in the body is input minus output.

why.correct: To lose heat, the skin's blood vessels dilate, bringing warm blood to the surface. Constriction would keep warm blood away from the skin and reduce heat loss, which is the response to cold.
options: This step is correct. A rise in temperature is the stimulus.
This step is correct. These nerve endings are the sensory receptors.
This step is correct. This is the afferent pathway to the control center.
This is the wrong step. A rise in temperature calls for vasodilation of skin vessels, not vasoconstriction.
This step is correct, but only if the vessels dilate. It is the response that opposes the stimulus.

why.correct: Information travels from the sensory receptor toward the control center along the afferent pathway (af- = toward).
options: The set point is the value the control center compares against. It is not a step the signal travels along.
Correct. The afferent pathway links the sensory receptor to the control center.
The regulated variable is what the stimulus changes and the response corrects. It is not a pathway.
A target cell is a cell with a receptor protein for a messenger. It is not a slot in the loop.

why.correct: Her sensors, pathways and control center work, so the command to lose heat is sent. Her effectors, the skin blood vessels and the sweat glands, respond weakly, and the heat load of the heat wave is larger than they can oppose. That is a homeostatic imbalance caused by overwhelmed effectors.
options: Her nerves and control center work normally, and her body is responding to the heat, so detection is intact.
The case says her nerves work normally. Signals are reaching the control center.
The control center works normally and is sending commands. The problem is how strongly the effectors carry them out.
Correct. Weak vasodilation and little sweat mean the effectors cannot match the heat load.

variables.name: Skin temperature in the first minute
variables.why: Cold air draws heat from your skin at once, before any loop has had time to respond. This fall is the stimulus.

variables.name: Blood flow to the skin after the loop has responded
variables.why: The control center signals the smooth muscle of skin blood vessels to contract, and vasoconstriction keeps warm blood away from the surface.

variables.name: Heat produced by skeletal muscles after the loop has responded
variables.why: Skeletal muscles, acting as effectors, contract in rapid small bursts (shivering), and those contractions release heat.

variables.name: Body temperature after an hour
variables.why: Reduced heat loss and increased heat production oppose the cooling, so negative feedback holds body temperature close to its set point, near where it started.

variables.name: Signals from the stretch-sensitive sensory receptors
variables.why: Lower pressure stretches the artery walls less, so the stretch-sensitive sensory receptors fire fewer action potentials; the control center reads this as a fall.

variables.name: Heart rate
variables.why: The control center sends signals along the efferent pathway that speed up the heart, which pumps more blood per minute and raises pressure.

variables.name: Diameter of small arteries
variables.why: The control center triggers vasoconstriction of small arteries. Narrower vessels raise resistance, which raises pressure back toward the set point.

why.correct: The control center (integrating center) receives the input, compares it with the set point, and sends commands along the efferent pathway.
options: Detecting the change is the job of the sensory receptor (sensor).
Carrying out the response is the job of the effector.
Correct. The control center compares the input with the set point and sends commands along the efferent pathway.
Carrying signals toward the control center is the job of the afferent pathway.

why.correct: Detecting a change, sending signals and getting effectors working all take time. By the time the response takes hold, the variable has moved, so the correction carries it slightly past the set point, and the loop then corrects the other way. The result is small swings within the normal range.
options: Correct. The time lag in a negative feedback loop means each correction carries the variable slightly past the set point, producing small oscillations.
Positive feedback would push temperature further away, not back. The small swings come from negative feedback.
The set point shifts slowly over the day, not randomly minute to minute, and that would not explain swings around it.
Sensory receptors keep reporting the variable; that is how the loop detects the next swing. Switching off is not the cause.

why.correct: Higher temperature causes more heat release, which raises temperature further: the response strengthens the stimulus. When negative feedback has failed, this harmful positive feedback loop can drive temperature up until cells are damaged, so outside cooling is needed.
options: Negative feedback has already failed to hold the temperature; the danger is that it is being overwhelmed, not that it overcorrects.
Correct. More heat causes more heat: a positive feedback loop that needs outside intervention to stop.
A set point does not fall to match a rising temperature. The problem is that the variable is being driven away from the set point.
Mass balance describes what happens when input and output differ; it does not force them to match. Here heat input exceeds output, so heat builds up.

why.correct: The efferent pathway carries the command from the control center to the effector. Here the command is a hormone carried in the blood from the kidneys to the bone marrow. An efferent pathway can be a hormone as well as a nerve.
options: The kidney cells that detect low oxygen act as the sensory receptor and the control center; they are not the pathway.
Correct. The hormone carries the command to the effector, so it is the efferent pathway.
More red blood cells carrying more oxygen is the response, not the pathway.
The bone marrow carries out the command, so it is the effector.

why.correct: In labor, stronger contractions cause more stretch, which causes more hormone release and stronger contractions still. The response strengthens the stimulus, which is positive feedback.
options: Body temperature is held near its set point by negative feedback: cold triggers responses that warm you.
Blood pressure is held by negative feedback: a fall triggers responses that raise it.
Blood pH is held by negative feedback: a fall triggers responses that raise it back toward 7.40.
Correct. Labor contractions build on themselves until delivery ends the loop.

why.correct: The heart sits in the mediastinum, the central compartment of the thoracic cavity. It lies between the lungs, behind the sternum, in front of the esophagus and vertebral column, and on the diaphragm.
options: The left pleural cavity surrounds the left lung. The heart leans to the left, but it stays in the mediastinum, medial to that cavity.

The abdominopelvic cavity lies below the diaphragm. The heart rests on top of the diaphragm, so it is above this cavity.
The dorsal body cavity holds the brain and spinal cord. The heart is in the ventral body cavity, in the thorax.

why.correct: The apex is the pointed lower end of the heart. It points inferiorly, anteriorly and to the left, and lies at about the fifth intercostal space on the left.
options: Correct. The pointed lower tip is the apex.
The base is the broad upper, back end where the large vessels attach, not the lower tip.
The pericardial cavity is the thin fluid-filled space between the two serous layers around the heart, not a part of the heart itself.
The mediastinum is the whole central compartment of the chest that holds the heart, not one end of it.

why.correct: The fibrous pericardium is the outermost layer. Its dense collagen anchors the heart and resists stretch.
options: The parietal pericardium is the serous layer fused to the inside of the fibrous pericardium. It is thin mesothelium, not tough dense connective tissue.
The epicardium is the visceral layer of the serous pericardium, on the surface of the heart. It is inside the pericardial cavity, not the outermost layer.
Correct. The tough outer bag is the fibrous pericardium.
The endocardium is the innermost layer of the heart wall, lining the spaces inside the heart.

why.correct: The epicardium lies on the outer surface of the myocardium, just inside the pericardial cavity. It is also called the visceral pericardium.
options: The parietal pericardium is on the outer side of the pericardial cavity, fused to the fibrous pericardium. The pinned layer is on the inner side.
Correct. The layer on the heart muscle, facing the pericardial cavity, is the epicardium (visceral pericardium).
The endocardium lines the inside of the heart, on the inner surface of the myocardium, far from the pericardial cavity.
The myocardium is the thick muscle layer itself, not the thin covering on it.

why.correct: Outside to inside: the tough fibrous pericardium, the parietal serous layer fused to it, the fluid film of the pericardial cavity, the epicardium on the heart surface, the thick myocardium, and finally the endocardium lining the inside.
options: The fibrous pericardium is the outermost bag, so the needle meets it first.
The parietal pericardium is fused to the inside of the fibrous pericardium, so it comes next.
The pericardial cavity is the fluid film between the parietal and visceral layers.
The epicardium is the visceral serous layer on the heart surface, the first layer of the heart wall.
The myocardium is the thick muscle in the middle of the wall.
The endocardium lines the inside of the heart, so it is the last layer before the blood.

why.correct: The myocardium is cardiac muscle tissue. It is the thickest layer, and its fibers shorten to squeeze blood out of the heart.
options: The epicardium is a thin covering of mesothelium and connective tissue. It holds surface vessels and fat but does not contract.
The endocardium is a thin endothelial lining. It gives blood a smooth surface but has no contractile muscle.
The fibrous pericardium is not part of the heart wall at all. It is the collagen bag around the heart.
Correct. The myocardium is the muscle layer that pumps.

why.correct: The fibrous pericardium is dense collagen and cannot expand fast. Blood collecting in the pericardial cavity therefore raises the pressure in the sac, which squeezes the heart and keeps it from filling fully between beats. That is cardiac tamponade.
options: A tear in the endocardium alone would not put blood around the heart, and the signs here come from compression from outside, not from a leak inside.
The epicardium does not thicken within minutes, and a stiffer wall is not what compresses the heart in this scenario.
Correct. The unyielding fibrous pericardium turns a small added volume into a large rise in pressure.
If the heart could balloon outward it would fill more, not less. The problem is that the heart is squeezed and cannot expand.

why.correct: The endocardium is lined by endothelium, and both layers of the serous pericardium (the epicardium and the parietal pericardium) are covered by mesothelium. Endothelium and mesothelium are both simple squamous epithelium.
options: Yes. The endocardium is endothelium, a simple squamous epithelium, on thin connective tissue.
Yes. The epicardium is the visceral serous layer, so its surface is mesothelium, a simple squamous epithelium.
Yes. The parietal pericardium is the other serous layer, also covered by mesothelium.
No. The fibrous pericardium is dense connective tissue, mostly collagen, with no epithelial surface of its own.
No. The myocardium is cardiac muscle tissue, not epithelium.

why.correct: The apex points inferiorly, anteriorly and to the left. In most adults it touches the chest wall at the fifth intercostal space, in line with the middle of the left clavicle.
options: The upper right side of the sternum is near the base, where the large vessels attach. The tip of the heart points down and left, away from here.
Correct. This is where the apex lies in most adults.
The upper sternum is above the heart's base. The apex is much lower and to the left.
The tenth intercostal space is below the diaphragm's dome, in the region of the upper abdomen. The heart rests on the diaphragm, so its tip is higher than this.

why.correct: Despite its name, the base is at the top and back of the heart. It faces toward the right shoulder, and the large vessels enter and leave there.
options: Correct. The base is the wide upper, posterior end where the large vessels attach.
This describes the apex, the lower tip, not the base.
The front surface of the heart faces the sternum, but the base faces mostly backward and upward.
This describes the pericardial cavity, a space outside the heart wall, not a part of the heart.

why.correct: Fluid in an unstretchable sac raises the pressure around the heart. The heart cannot fill, so it pumps out less, blood pressure falls, and blood backs up in the veins.

variables.name: Pressure inside the pericardial sac
variables.why: Added volume in a sac whose fibrous layer cannot stretch quickly raises the pressure inside it.

variables.name: How much blood fills the heart between beats
variables.why: The high pressure outside the heart squeezes its thin-walled parts, so less blood can flow in between beats.

variables.name: Blood pressure
variables.why: A heart that fills less pumps out less blood with each beat, so blood pressure falls.

variables.name: Bulging of the neck veins
variables.why: Blood returning to the heart cannot get into the squeezed heart, so it backs up in the large veins, including those in the neck.

why.correct: Collagen in the fibrous pericardium cannot stretch fast, so a small, rapid volume causes a steep pressure rise. Over weeks the tissue remodels and the sac enlarges, so a large, slow volume can fit with little rise in pressure. Rate matters more than volume.
options: A weaker muscle would make the heart more vulnerable to outside compression, not less, and nothing in the scenario says the muscle is weak.
Any fluid in a closed sac exerts pressure. What matters is how much the sac's pressure rises, which depends on how fast it can enlarge.
If the layers had fused there would be no cavity for 900 mL of fluid to fill, so this cannot explain Patient B.
Correct. Slow accumulation gives the fibrous pericardium time to enlarge; rapid accumulation does not.

why.correct: The heart wall has three layers: epicardium outside, myocardium in the middle and endocardium inside.
options: Correct. The myocardium, the muscle layer, sits between the epicardium and the endocardium.
The pericardial cavity lies outside the epicardium, between it and the parietal pericardium. It is not inside the heart wall.
The fibrous pericardium is the outermost covering, outside the whole heart wall.
The parietal pericardium lines the fibrous pericardium, outside the pericardial cavity, not within the heart wall.

why.correct: The fibrous pericardium is dense collagen and cannot stretch quickly. Because it does not give way, added fluid raises the pressure in the sac and squeezes the heart.
options: This step is correct. Tamponade starts when fluid enters the cavity faster than it can leave.
This is the wrong step. The fibrous pericardium resists stretch, and that is exactly why pressure builds.
This step is correct. The raised pressure acts on the heart's outer surface.
This step is correct. A compressed heart cannot fill fully, so each beat sends out less blood.
This step is correct. Less blood pumped lowers blood pressure, and blood returning to the heart backs up in the veins.

why.correct: The fibrous pericardium is dense connective tissue, packed with collagen fibers. That is why it is tough and resists stretching.
options: Simple squamous epithelium (mesothelium) covers the serous layers, not the fibrous pericardium.
Cardiac muscle tissue forms the myocardium. The pericardium has no muscle.
Correct. Dense collagen makes the fibrous pericardium strong and hard to stretch.
Loose tissue with fat lies under the epicardium, on the heart surface. It is not the tough outer bag.

why.correct: The fluid sits in the pericardial cavity. From outside, the needle must cross the fibrous pericardium and the parietal layer fused to it. Past those, it is in the fluid. It should stop before the epicardium, which is the surface of the heart.
options: The epicardium and myocardium are the heart wall itself. Piercing them means the needle has gone past the fluid and into the heart.
The endocardium lines the inside of the heart. A needle reaching it has passed through the entire heart wall.
Correct. The fibrous and parietal layers form the outer wall of the pericardial cavity.
These are the inner layers of the heart wall. Reaching them means the needle is inside the heart, not in the pericardial fluid.

why.correct: The epicardium is the visceral layer of the serous pericardium. One sheet of tissue carries both names, so there is no separate layer between them.
options: The visceral pericardium is on the heart's outer surface. Inside the myocardium is the endocardium.
Correct. The epicardium is the visceral pericardium.
The fibrous pericardium is the outermost layer. The epicardium lies deep to it, on the heart itself.
The visceral pericardium is a serous membrane: mesothelium on thin connective tissue. Dense connective tissue describes the fibrous pericardium.

why.correct: Normally a film of serous fluid lets the parietal and visceral layers slide silently. When the layers are rough and poorly lubricated, they rub against each other with every beat, producing a scratching sound.
options: Friction between the layers does not stop the heart. The heart keeps beating, and the rubbing makes a sound.
Correct. Roughened layers with less fluid rub together, which makes a scratchy sound.
Less fluid removes lubrication, which adds a sound rather than just sharpening the normal one.
Inflammation does not bring air into the pericardial cavity. The sound comes from rubbing tissue.

why.correct: The heart sits on the diaphragm, between the lungs, with about two thirds of its mass left of the midline. It lies in front of the esophagus, and its apex points down and to the left.
options: Correct. The heart's lower surface rests on the diaphragm.
Correct. The heart is tilted so most of its mass is left of the midline.
Incorrect. The esophagus lies behind the heart, so the heart is anterior to it.
Incorrect. The base faces toward the right shoulder. The apex points down, forward and to the left.
Correct. The two lungs lie on either side of the mediastinum, which holds the heart.

why.correct: The pulmonary trunk is the short, wide vessel leaving the top of the right ventricle at the front of the base. It splits into the right and left pulmonary arteries, one to each lung.
options: The superior vena cava comes down into the right atrium on the heart's right side (the left of the drawing). It does not leave the front of the ventricles.
The arch of the aorta curves up, back and to the left above the heart, over the top of the pinned vessel.
The left auricle is the ear-shaped pouch of the left atrium, lying just beside the pinned vessel. It is part of a chamber, not a vessel.
Correct. This is the pulmonary trunk, leaving the right ventricle.

why.correct: The inferior vena cava carries blood from everything below the diaphragm and opens into the right atrium. A catheter following that vein reaches the right atrium first.
options: Correct. Both venae cavae empty into the right atrium.
The left atrium receives the pulmonary veins from the lungs, not the venae cavae.
The right ventricle lies below the right atrium and receives blood from it. The catheter would have to pass through the right atrium first.
The left ventricle receives blood from the left atrium and sends it out through the aorta. No vein opens into it.

why.correct: Blood low in oxygen returns from the body's tissues through the two venae cavae into the right atrium. The right ventricle sends it out through the pulmonary trunk and pulmonary arteries to the lungs. Blood that has picked up oxygen in the lungs returns through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium and leaves the left ventricle through the aorta.
options: Yes. The superior vena cava returns blood from the head, neck, arms and upper chest after the tissues have taken oxygen from it.
No. The pulmonary veins carry blood that has just picked up oxygen in the lungs back to the left atrium.
Yes. The pulmonary trunk carries blood from the right ventricle toward the lungs, before it picks up oxygen.
No. The aorta carries blood rich in oxygen from the left ventricle out to the body.
Yes. The inferior vena cava returns blood from below the diaphragm after the tissues have taken oxygen from it.
Yes. The pulmonary arteries are the two branches of the pulmonary trunk, carrying blood low in oxygen to the lungs.

why.correct: An artery carries blood away from the heart and a vein carries blood toward it. Oxygen content plays no part in the definition. The pulmonary veins carry blood toward the heart, so they are veins even though that blood has just picked up oxygen in the lungs.
options: The pulmonary veins carry blood that has just passed through the lungs, so it is rich in oxygen. The student has the oxygen right; the definition is what is wrong.
Draining into a chamber does not make a vessel part of the heart. The venae cavae drain into the right atrium and are still veins.
Correct. Direction relative to the heart, not oxygen content, decides whether a vessel is an artery or a vein.
The same rule applies everywhere: the pulmonary trunk and aorta both carry blood away from the heart and are both arteries.

why.correct: The valve between the left atrium and the left ventricle is the mitral valve (also called the bicuspid valve). It has two cusps.
options: The tricuspid valve sits between the right atrium and the right ventricle, on the other side of the heart.
The aortic valve sits at the exit from the left ventricle into the aorta, not between the left atrium and ventricle.
The pulmonary valve sits at the exit from the right ventricle into the pulmonary trunk.
Correct. This is the mitral valve, the left atrioventricular valve.

why.correct: Chordae tendineae are collagen cords that tie the cusps of the atrioventricular valves to the papillary muscles.
options: Pectinate muscles are comb-like muscle ridges in the atria, not cords attached to valve cusps.
Correct. These cords are the chordae tendineae.
Trabeculae carneae are ridges of muscle on the ventricle walls. They are thick muscle, not thin cords.
Papillary muscles are the cones of muscle that the cords attach to, not the cords themselves.

why.correct: The fossa ovalis is a shallow oval depression in the interatrial septum, seen from the right atrium.
options: The coronary sulcus is a groove on the outside of the heart between the atria and ventricles, not a dip inside the atrial wall.
Correct. The oval dip in the interatrial septum is the fossa ovalis.
An auricle is an ear-shaped pouch on the front of each atrium, not a dip in the septum.
The atrioventricular septum lies between the atria and the ventricles, not between the two atria.

why.correct: The pulmonary valve is the most anterior of the four valves. It is a semilunar valve with three half-moon cusps, at the exit from the right ventricle.
options: The aortic valve also has three half-moon cusps, but it sits behind the pulmonary valve, closer to the center of the heart.
The mitral valve has two flat cusps and lies at the back left, not in front.

The tricuspid valve has three flat cusps held by cords, and it lies at the back right.

why.correct: The cusps hang into the ventricle, the chordae tendineae run from the cusp edges down to the papillary muscles, and the papillary muscles rise from the ventricle's myocardium.
options: The cusps sit at the opening itself.
The chordae tendineae attach to the free edges of the cusps.
The papillary muscle anchors the lower ends of the cords.
The papillary muscle is an extension of the ventricle wall's myocardium.

why.correct: The semilunar valves are the pulmonary and aortic valves. Each has three pocket-shaped cusps and guards the exit from a ventricle into its artery. They have no cords or muscles.
options: Yes. Each semilunar valve has three half-moon cusps shaped like pockets.
No. Chordae tendineae hold the atrioventricular valves. Semilunar cusps have no cords.
Yes. The semilunar valves sit where each ventricle empties into its artery.
Yes. The pulmonary valve and the aortic valve are the two semilunar valves.
No. That location belongs to the atrioventricular valves, the tricuspid and the mitral.

why.correct: Papillary muscles contract with the ventricle and pull the chordae tendineae tight, which stops the mitral cusps flipping up into the atrium. With one torn, the cusps it held swing up when the ventricle squeezes, and blood leaks backward into the left atrium.
options: Papillary muscles do not open the valve. Blood pushes the cusps open. Their job is to keep the closed cusps from flipping up, so losing one causes backward leak, not a stuck valve.
Correct. Without the anchor, the cusps flip into the left atrium and blood flows backward with every contraction.
The aortic valve is a semilunar valve with no papillary muscles, so a torn papillary muscle does not affect it directly.
The tricuspid valve is on the right side of the heart. Mrs. Okafor's torn muscle is in the left ventricle.

why.correct: The vessels of the whole body resist flow far more than those of the lungs. To push the same volume through them, the left ventricle must raise pressure to about 120 mm Hg, versus about 25 mm Hg on the right. Muscle that works against a heavier load thickens.
options: On average, both ventricles pump the same volume each beat. If they did not, blood would pile up on one side within minutes.
Distance alone is not the cause. What sets the work is the pressure needed to overcome the resistance of the vessels.
Blood on both sides is the same blood, with the same thickness. It passes through the right side first and the left side next.
Correct. The higher pressure load on the left ventricle is what thickens its wall.

why.correct: Snapped cords let the mitral cusps flip, so the ventricle pushes some blood backward. More goes into the left atrium, raising its pressure, and less goes forward into the aorta.

variables.why: Without the cords to hold them, the mitral cusps flip up into the left atrium when the ventricle squeezes, so blood leaks backward through the gap.

variables.name: Volume of blood the left ventricle sends into the aorta each beat
variables.why: Some of the blood the ventricle squeezes goes backward into the atrium instead of forward, so less leaves through the aortic valve.

variables.name: Pressure in the left atrium
variables.why: Extra blood pushed back into the left atrium on top of the blood arriving from the pulmonary veins raises the pressure inside it.

why.correct: The tricuspid valve is the right atrioventricular valve. It lets blood pass from the right atrium down into the right ventricle, which then pumps out through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk.
options: Correct. The tricuspid valve sits between the right atrium and the right ventricle.
The mitral valve is the left atrioventricular valve, between the left atrium and the left ventricle.
The aortic valve guards the exit from the left ventricle into the aorta, on the other side of the heart.
The interatrial septum is the wall between the two atria. Blood does not pass through it on its way to the right ventricle.

why.correct: The valve between the left atrium and the left ventricle is the mitral valve. The tricuspid valve is on the right side, between the right atrium and right ventricle.
options: Correct step. The pulmonary veins deliver blood from the lungs to the left atrium.
Correct step. The left atrium is the receiving chamber on the left side.
This is the wrong step. The left atrioventricular valve is the mitral valve, not the tricuspid.
Correct step. The left ventricle lies below the left atrium.
Correct step. The aortic valve guards the exit from the left ventricle.
Correct step. The aorta carries blood out of the left ventricle.

why.correct: The cardiac skeleton is dense collagen lying between the atria and the ventricles. Collagen does not conduct electrical signals like muscle does, so the signal can cross only at one specialized pathway.
options: The interventricular septum separates the right and left ventricles, so it lies between the two pumping chambers rather than between the atria and the ventricles.
Correct. The dense connective tissue of the cardiac skeleton insulates the atria from the ventricles.
The pericardial sac surrounds the whole heart on the outside. It does not sit between the atria and the ventricles.
The chordae tendineae are cords inside the ventricles that hold valve cusps. They do not block electrical signals between chambers.

why.correct: Trabeculae carneae are ridges and bridges of muscle on the inner walls of the ventricles.
options: Correct. They line the inner walls of the ventricles.
The auricles are lined by pectinate muscles, the comb-like ridges of the atria.
Semilunar cusps are thin pockets of endocardium and connective tissue, with no muscle ridges.
The surface grooves are the sulci, filled with fat and surface vessels.

why.correct: Semilunar valves have pocket-shaped cusps. Blood slipping back toward the ventricle fills the pockets, and the cusps bulge together and seal. No cords or muscles are involved, so a replacement needs none.
options: No muscle opens or closes any heart valve. Blood moving against the cusps does it.

Blood does start to flow back toward the ventricle when it relaxes. That backflow is what fills the pockets and closes the valve.
Papillary muscles attach only to the atrioventricular valves through the chordae tendineae, not to semilunar cusps.

why.correct: The interventricular septum is the thick, mostly muscular wall between the right and left ventricles. It runs from the valves down toward the apex.
options: The interatrial septum is the thin wall between the two atria, higher up in the heart.
The atrioventricular septum is the region between the atria and the ventricles, where the valve openings pass through. It runs across the heart, not down between the ventricles.
Correct. The thick wall between the two ventricles is the interventricular septum.
Trabeculae carneae are ridges of muscle on the inner walls of the ventricles, not the wall that divides them.

why.correct: The wall between the atria is the interatrial septum. On its right atrial side is the fossa ovalis, a shallow oval dip with a thinner floor than the rest of the septum.
options: Chordae tendineae run from the atrioventricular valve cusps down to papillary muscles in the ventricles. They are not on the wall between the atria.
Trabeculae carneae ridge the inner walls of the ventricles, not the atria. The atria have pectinate muscles in their auricles instead.
Correct. The fossa ovalis sits on the right atrial side of the interatrial septum.
The pulmonary trunk leaves the right ventricle, through the pulmonary valve. It does not open from the atrial wall.

why.correct: The collagen rings of the cardiac skeleton hold each valve opening at a fixed size. If a ring stretches, the opening widens while the cusps stay the same size, so the cusps no longer meet when the valve closes and blood leaks backward through it.
options: The rings are still collagen, so they still block electrical signals from crossing straight from the atria to the ventricles. A wider opening does not change the order of contraction.
Stretched valve rings do not thin the ventricle walls. Wall thickness follows the pressure a ventricle works against.
Papillary muscles are part of the ventricle wall and contract with it. Weak collagen in the valve rings does not stop that.
Correct. A widened opening leaves a gap between cusps that are no longer big enough to meet.

why.correct: The interatrial septum is a thin wall between the atria and carries the fossa ovalis. The interventricular septum is a thick, mostly muscular wall between the ventricles. The atrioventricular septum is the region between the atria above and the ventricles below.
options: Correct. The interventricular septum is thick and mostly muscle, with a small, thin fibrous part near the top.
Correct. The interatrial septum is the wall between the right and left atria.
Incorrect. The atrioventricular septum lies between the atria and the ventricles. The wall between the two ventricles is the interventricular septum.

why.correct: Blood from the legs returns through the inferior vena cava to the right atrium. The right ventricle pumps it to the pulmonary capillaries, where it picks up oxygen. It returns through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium, and the left ventricle pumps it into the aorta.

The right atrium passes blood through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, which pumps it toward the lungs.
The right ventricle pumps blood through the pulmonary trunk and arteries to the pulmonary capillaries, where it becomes oxygenated.
The pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood from the lungs into the left atrium.
The left atrium passes blood through the mitral valve into the left ventricle.
The left ventricle pumps blood through the aortic valve into the aorta, so the aorta comes last.

why.correct: The anterior interventricular artery, usually called the left anterior descending artery, is a branch of the left coronary artery that runs down the anterior interventricular sulcus toward the apex.
options: The circumflex artery curves around the left side of the heart in the coronary sulcus. It does not run down the front toward the apex.
The right coronary artery runs around the right side of the heart in the coronary sulcus, not down the front groove.
Correct. This is the anterior interventricular artery (left anterior descending).
The posterior interventricular artery runs down the groove between the ventricles on the back of the heart, not the front.

why.correct: The left anterior descending (anterior interventricular) artery runs down the front of the heart. It supplies the front of the left ventricle, the front two thirds of the interventricular septum and the apex, so those regions lose their blood supply.
options: Correct. This is the territory of the left anterior descending artery.
The right atrium and most of the right ventricle are fed by the right coronary artery, which is not blocked here.
The back of both ventricles is fed by the posterior interventricular artery, which in most people comes from the right coronary artery.
The left atrium and the side wall of the left ventricle are fed by the circumflex artery, the other branch of the left coronary artery.

why.correct: Heart muscle removes about 70 to 75 percent of the oxygen from the blood reaching it, far more than most tissues remove. The coronary sinus collects that blood, so it is the most deoxygenated blood in the body at rest.
options: Blood in a pulmonary vein has just left the lungs, so it is fully oxygenated.
Blood in the aorta is oxygenated blood that the left ventricle has just pumped out.
Blood in the right atrium is deoxygenated, but it mixes blood from all tissues, and most tissues take only about a quarter of the oxygen. It still holds more oxygen than blood draining heart muscle.
Correct. Blood leaving heart muscle has given up most of its oxygen.

why.correct: A faster heart rate shortens diastole the most, which cuts the time for coronary flow into the left ventricle's wall, while the harder-working muscle uses more oxygen.

variables.name: Length of each ventricular diastole
variables.why: Each cycle falls from 0.8 to 0.4 seconds, and nearly all of that cut comes out of diastole, which falls from about 0.5 to 0.15 seconds.

variables.name: Time per minute available for blood to flow into the left ventricle's muscle
variables.why: Most flow into the left ventricle's wall happens in diastole, when the relaxed muscle stops squeezing its vessels, and the total time spent in diastole each minute falls.

variables.name: Oxygen used by the heart muscle each minute
variables.why: Twice as many contractions each minute use more ATP, so the muscle's aerobic respiration and oxygen use rise.

why.correct: The pulmonary and systemic circuits are connected in series: all the blood the right ventricle sends through the lungs returns to the left side. So over time the two ventricles pump the same volume, even though the left makes about five times the pressure.
options: If the left ventricle pumped only 1 liter while the right pumped 5, about 4 liters a minute would pile up in the lungs.
Correct. In series circuits, both pumps move the same volume per minute.
The left ventricle makes more pressure, not more volume. Pumping twice as much as the right would drain the lungs within minutes.
This multiplies the volume by the pressure ratio. Pressure and volume are different quantities: higher pressure does not mean a larger volume.

why.correct: Oxygenated blood runs from the lungs through the pulmonary veins to the left heart, then out through the aorta and its branches, including the coronary arteries.
options: Yes. The pulmonary veins carry blood that has just picked up oxygen in the lungs back to the left atrium.
No. The pulmonary trunk carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle toward the lungs.
Yes. The left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood into the aorta.
No. The superior vena cava returns deoxygenated blood from the upper body to the right atrium.
Yes. The coronary arteries are the first branches of the aorta, so they carry the same oxygenated blood.

why.correct: A narrowed coronary artery supplies enough blood at rest but not when exertion raises the muscle's oxygen use. The ischemia causes pain, and it reverses once demand falls. This is angina. Normal troponin fits: no muscle has died.
options: Dying muscle is a myocardial infarction. Pain from an infarction usually lasts longer and does not ease with rest, and dying fibers release troponin, which is normal here.
Correct. This is angina: ischemia that reverses when oxygen demand falls.
Blood filling the pericardial sac would squeeze the heart and lower blood pressure, and it would not come and go with stair climbing.
In a healthy adult heart the right and left sides do not share blood. Nothing in her story suggests a hole between the chambers.

why.correct: The right ventricle pumps through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk, toward the lungs. The aortic valve and the aorta belong to the left ventricle.
options: This step is correct. Both venae cavae empty into the right atrium.
This step is correct. The tricuspid valve lies between the right atrium and the right ventricle.
This is the wrong step. The right ventricle pumps through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk; the aortic valve guards the exit from the left ventricle.
This step is correct. The pulmonary veins bring oxygenated blood into the left atrium.
This step is correct. The mitral valve lies between the left atrium and the left ventricle.

why.correct: The great cardiac vein drains into the coronary sinus, the wide vein in the coronary sulcus on the back of the heart. The coronary sinus empties into the right atrium.
options: The pulmonary veins carry blood from the lungs. The heart's own veins do not drain into them.
The anterior cardiac veins are separate small veins on the front of the right ventricle, and they empty into the right atrium, not the right ventricle.
Blood does not enter the left ventricle through the aortic valve; that valve lets blood out of the ventricle into the aorta.
Correct. Great cardiac vein, then coronary sinus, then right atrium.

why.correct: Branches of the coronary arteries dive into the myocardium. In systole the contracting muscle, especially in the thick left ventricle wall, compresses those vessels and slows flow. In diastole the muscle relaxes, the vessels open, and most flow occurs.
options: The coronary artery openings do not close. The limit on flow comes from the vessels inside the wall being squeezed.
Blood in the chamber reaches only a thin inner layer of muscle next to the endocardium. The rest of the wall depends on the coronary arteries.
Correct. The muscle compresses its own vessels as it contracts, like squeezing a garden hose.
Heart muscle uses oxygen all the time, and most of all while it contracts. Its supply, not its use, is what falls in systole.

why.correct: The mitral valve is the left atrioventricular valve, between the left atrium and the left ventricle.
options: Correct. Blood crosses the mitral valve from the left atrium into the left ventricle.
The tricuspid valve lies on the right side, between the right atrium and the right ventricle.
The pulmonary valve guards the exit from the right ventricle into the pulmonary trunk.
The coronary sinus is a vein on the back of the heart that drains the heart wall into the right atrium, not a valve.

why.correct: At rest, tissues take only about a quarter of the oxygen that arrives, so returning blood is still about 75 percent loaded. It is dark red. Veins look blue through the skin because of how skin scatters and absorbs light.
options: No blood in the body is blue, whatever its oxygen content.
Deoxygenated blood still carries a lot of oxygen; at rest the tissues remove only about a quarter of it.
Correct. Deoxygenated blood is dark red and still carries most of its oxygen at rest.
Bright red, fully loaded blood is oxygenated blood leaving the lungs, not blood returning in a vein from the hand.

why.correct: The heart has small anastomoses between coronary branches. When an artery narrows slowly, more blood is pushed through these connections and they widen over months, forming collateral circulation. When the artery finally closes, collaterals can still feed much of the region. Patient B had no time to develop them.
options: Correct. Slow narrowing drives collateral circulation to develop through anastomoses.
Heart muscle depends on aerobic respiration and cannot switch to working without oxygen for long, however slowly a block develops.
Veins carry blood away from the heart muscle. They do not reverse and supply it.
In a healthy adult heart the interventricular septum is a solid wall, and even if blood crossed it, it would not reach the blocked artery's territory.

why.correct: The coronary sinus lies in the coronary sulcus on the back of the heart. The great, middle, small and posterior cardiac veins empty into it, and it empties into the right atrium.
options: The great cardiac vein empties into the coronary sinus. It is one of its tributaries, not the wide collecting vein itself.
The inferior vena cava enters the right atrium from below and drains the lower body, not the heart wall.
Correct. This is the coronary sinus.
The posterior interventricular artery runs down the groove between the ventricles on the back. It is an artery, not a collecting vein in the groove around the heart.

why.correct: The pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood from the lungs into the left atrium. They are veins because they carry blood toward the heart.
options: The pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood away from the right ventricle to the lungs.
The aorta carries oxygenated blood away from the left ventricle to the body.
The venae cavae return deoxygenated blood from the body to the right atrium.
Correct. These are the pulmonary veins.

why.correct: One cycle lasts 60 s ÷ 50 beats = 1.2 s. Subtract systole: 1.2 s − 0.3 s = 0.9 s of diastole.
options: 0.5 seconds is the diastole for a heart rate of 75 beats per minute, when each cycle lasts 0.8 seconds.
0.3 seconds is the length of systole, not diastole.
1.2 seconds is the whole cycle. Systole still has to be subtracted.
Correct. 1.2 s per cycle minus 0.3 s of systole leaves 0.9 s.

why.correct: In this pattern, the back of both ventricles is fed by a branch of the circumflex artery, which comes from the left coronary artery. A block of the left coronary artery before it branches cuts off the circumflex, and so the posterior interventricular artery too.
options: In this person the right coronary artery does not give rise to the posterior interventricular artery, so a block there would spare the back of the ventricles.
Correct. The left coronary artery feeds the circumflex, which here feeds the posterior interventricular artery.
The marginal arteries feed the right edge of the heart, not the back of both ventricles.
The coronary sinus is a vein that drains blood away. Blocking it does not stop arterial supply to the back of the ventricles.

why.correct: Flow depends on the pressure difference and the resistance. The pulmonary circuit's vessels are short, wide and numerous, so they resist flow little, and a small pressure moves the full volume. The systemic vessels resist much more, so the left ventricle needs about 120 mm Hg.
options: Correct. Low resistance in the pulmonary circuit means a small pressure moves the same volume.
Distance matters only through resistance. Pressure still drives flow in both circuits; the lungs simply resist it less.
Oxygen content does not noticeably change how thick blood is. The same blood flows through both circuits.
Valves only let blood through in one direction. They do not add pressure.

why.correct: Starved muscle fibers cannot run aerobic respiration fully, so they make less ATP and shift to anaerobic metabolism, producing lactate. Lactate, other acids and chemicals from the ischemic muscle stimulate pain-sensing nerve endings.
options: Correct. Ischemia leads to lactate and other chemicals, which stimulate pain nerve endings.
A blocked artery does not stretch or tear the pericardium. The pain comes from the starved muscle itself.
A coronary block does not simply stop the heartbeat, and the pain comes from chemicals released by ischemic muscle, not from the heart pausing.
A blocked artery lowers, not raises, the oxygen reaching the muscle downstream.

why.correct: The coronary arteries are the first branches of the aorta. The left coronary artery gives off the anterior interventricular artery, which feeds capillaries in the front wall of the left ventricle. The great cardiac vein collects that blood and empties into the coronary sinus, which drains into the right atrium.
options: The left coronary artery leaves the aorta just above the aortic valve. It is short and splits almost at once.
The anterior interventricular artery is one of its two branches and runs down the front of the heart.
Its branches dive into the myocardium and end in capillaries, where oxygen leaves the blood.
The great cardiac vein runs up beside the anterior interventricular artery and collects that blood.
The great cardiac vein empties into the coronary sinus on the back of the heart.
The coronary sinus empties into the right atrium, which ends the loop.

why.correct: In systemic capillaries, cells use oxygen and make carbon dioxide, so oxygen moves down its gradient out of the blood and carbon dioxide moves into it. At rest the tissue takes only about a quarter of the oxygen.
options: Yes. Cells use oxygen, so it is lower in the tissue and diffuses out of the blood.
Yes. Cells make carbon dioxide, so it is higher in the tissue and diffuses into the blood.
No. Oxygen moves into the blood in the pulmonary capillaries, not in the tissues.
Yes. At rest, blood leaving the tissues is still about 75 percent loaded with oxygen.
No. Carbon dioxide moves out of the blood in the lungs, where it is lower in the air of the alveoli than in the blood.

why.correct: At threshold, voltage-gated sodium channels open and sodium rushes in down its electrochemical gradient, taking the membrane from about −70 mV to about +20 mV in about a millisecond. This is the same fast upstroke as in neurons and skeletal muscle.
options: L-type calcium channels open too slowly to carry a millisecond-long upstroke. Calcium entry holds the plateau that follows.
Correct. Fast sodium entry carries phase 0.
Potassium leaving makes the inside more negative. It carries repolarization in phase 3, not the upstroke.
Calcium released from the SR goes into the cytosol, not across the plasma membrane, so it does not change the membrane potential's upstroke. It activates contraction.

why.correct: During the plateau, L-type calcium channels let positive charge in as calcium while potassium channels let positive charge out as potassium. The two currents nearly cancel, so the voltage barely changes.
options: The sodium channels inactivate within a millisecond or two of the upstroke and stay inactivated through the plateau.
Ions are moving in both directions throughout the plateau. The voltage is flat because the movements balance, not because they stop.
The sodium–potassium pump runs throughout. Its small current does not create the plateau.
Correct. Inward calcium current roughly equals outward potassium current.

why.correct: Blocking L-type channels shrinks the calcium trigger, so calcium-induced calcium release falls and each contraction weakens. The sodium upstroke is unaffected.

variables.name: Calcium entering the cell during the plateau
variables.why: The blocked L-type channels are the path calcium takes into the cell during the plateau, so less enters.

variables.name: Calcium released by the sarcoplasmic reticulum each beat
variables.why: Entering calcium is the trigger that opens the SR's release channels, so a smaller trigger opens fewer of them and less calcium is released.

variables.name: Force of each contraction
variables.why: Less calcium in the cytosol binds less troponin, so fewer cross-bridges form and each contraction is weaker.

variables.name: Height of the phase 0 upstroke
variables.why: The upstroke is carried by sodium through voltage-gated sodium channels, which the drug does not block.

why.correct: Raising extracellular calcium steepens the gradient for calcium entry, so more calcium flows in through the channels that are still open. The larger trigger opens more SR release channels, more calcium reaches troponin, and more cross-bridges form.
options: Correct. More calcium entering means a larger trigger for calcium-induced calcium release.
Calcium in the blood does not strengthen the sodium upstroke, and the upstroke does not set the force of contraction.
The SR's release channels face the cytosol, not the blood. Calcium from the blood has to enter the cell first, through L-type channels.
A longer refractory period would not strengthen contraction; force depends on how much calcium reaches troponin.

why.correct: Charge from a neighbor brings the cell to threshold; the sodium upstroke depolarizes it; depolarization opens L-type channels; entering calcium opens the SR's release channels; the SR floods the cytosol with calcium; calcium binds troponin and the cell contracts.
options: The action potential reaches the cell as charge from a neighbor that has already fired.
That charge depolarizes the cell to threshold, and voltage-gated sodium channels open for the upstroke.
The depolarization slowly opens L-type calcium channels, and calcium enters during the plateau.
The entering calcium crosses a narrow gap and opens the SR's calcium release channels.
The SR releases far more calcium than entered: calcium-induced calcium release.
Calcium binding troponin moves tropomyosin aside, and cross-bridges form.

why.correct: The sodium channels stay inactivated through the whole plateau, so the absolute refractory period lasts about 200 to 250 ms, nearly as long as the contraction. No new action potential can start until the cell is already relaxing, so twitches cannot add up into tetanus.
options: Correct. The long refractory period prevents wave summation and tetanus.
Even with a smaller SR, cardiac muscle cells get enough calcium for strong contractions. The limit is electrical, not a shortage of calcium.
Fast spread through gap junctions does not stop a cell from being restimulated. What stops it is that the cell cannot fire again until its refractory period ends.
Heart muscle makes ATP continuously by aerobic respiration. The lack of tetanus comes from the refractory period, not from an ATP limit.

why.correct: Intercalated discs join cardiac muscle cells end to end. Each disc holds desmosomes and gap junctions.
options: The sarcoplasmic reticulum is a network of membrane sacs inside each cell that stores calcium. It does not join two cells.
The sarcolemma is the plasma membrane of each cell. An intercalated disc is where two cells' membranes meet and are joined.
A T tubule is an inward fold of the sarcolemma that carries the action potential into the cell, not a junction between cells.
Correct. This is an intercalated disc.

why.correct: Gap junctions are clusters of channels that link the cytoplasm of two neighboring cells, so ions and charge pass directly from one to the other.
options: Desmosomes anchor the two cells together mechanically. They do not form channels between them.
Tight junctions seal the spaces between epithelial cells. They are not the channels in cardiac intercalated discs.
Correct. Gap junctions connect the two cells' cytoplasm.
The intercalated disc is the whole junction. The pin marks one kind of junction within it.

why.correct: A contractile cell fires only when charge from a neighbor brings it to threshold. That charge travels through gap junctions. With them closed, the charge cannot pass, so the neighbors stay at rest.
options: Closing gap junctions does not change a cell's threshold. It stops the charge that would reach it.
If a neighbor did fire, its own L-type channels would still produce a plateau. The problem is that it never reaches threshold.
Correct. Without gap junctions, the action potential cannot spread from cell to cell.
The first cell's own channels still work, so it repolarizes normally when its potassium channels open.

why.correct: Midway through the plateau, calcium enters through open L-type channels while potassium leaves, keeping the membrane near 0 mV. The sodium channels are inactivated, which is why the cell is refractory.
options: Yes. Calcium entering through L-type channels holds the plateau.
Yes. Potassium leaving roughly balances the calcium entering.
Yes. The sodium channels inactivated just after the upstroke and stay that way while the membrane is depolarized.
No. The membrane is near 0 mV during the plateau. It is near −90 mV at rest.
No. Inactivated sodium channels cannot reopen until the membrane repolarizes, so the cell is in its absolute refractory period.

why.correct: Phase 3 repolarization is carried by potassium leaving the cell, as the L-type calcium channels close and more potassium channels open. Calcium does not rush out through channels; it is removed slowly by pumps and an exchanger.
options: This step is correct. At rest, potassium leak channels hold the membrane near −90 mV.
This step is correct. Fast sodium entry carries the upstroke.
This step is correct. A brief potassium current makes the small notch after the peak.
This step is correct. Balanced calcium entry and potassium exit hold the plateau.
This is the wrong step. Potassium leaving, not calcium, repolarizes the membrane in phase 3.

why.correct: Phase 2 is the plateau. Calcium entering through L-type channels balances potassium leaving, and the membrane stays near 0 mV for about 200 ms.
options: The membrane stays near 0 mV in phase 2. It does not go below the resting potential.
Sodium channels stay inactivated through the plateau. They recover only as the membrane repolarizes in phase 3.
Correct. The plateau follows the notch.
There is only one sodium upstroke. The sodium channels are inactivated during phase 2.

why.correct: The shortest possible time between upstrokes is 0.2 s. That gives 1 ÷ 0.2 s = 5 per second, and 5 × 60 = 300 per minute.
options: 200 is the refractory period in milliseconds, not a rate.
Correct. 5 per second times 60 seconds is 300 per minute.
500 per minute would mean one action potential every 0.12 s, which is shorter than this cell's 0.2 s refractory period allows.
120 per minute would mean one action potential every 0.5 s, far slower than the refractory period allows.

why.correct: Blocking the repolarizing potassium channels prolongs the plateau, which keeps the sodium channels inactivated longer, lengthening the refractory period and lowering the maximum firing rate.

variables.name: Duration of the action potential
variables.why: With less potassium leaving, outward current takes longer to overcome calcium entry, so the plateau lasts longer and repolarization is slower.

variables.name: Length of the absolute refractory period
variables.why: The sodium channels stay inactivated as long as the membrane stays depolarized, so a longer action potential means a longer refractory period.

variables.name: Fastest possible rate of action potentials
variables.why: A new action potential cannot start until the refractory period ends, so a longer refractory period lowers the ceiling on the rate.
